children.title: Convex Epigraph Geometry
children.top_down_role: Upper graph sets and their convex modeling role.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Epigraph Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real epigraph characterization of convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). The epigraph of \(f\) relative to \(C\) is \[\operatorname{epi}_C f=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)\le t\}.\] The function \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}_C f\) is convex. Consequently, an inequality \(f(x)\le t\) with convex \(f\) is a convex upper-graph constraint in the lifted variables \((x,t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph consists of points lying on or above a function’s graph. A function is convex exactly when its epigraph is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex.
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is convex}\iff\operatorname{epi}_C f\text{ is convex}.\)

notation.meaning: Epigraph of f relative to C.

children.title: Concave Hypograph Geometry
children.top_down_role: Lower graph sets and their concave modeling role.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave Hypograph Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real hypograph characterization of concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(g:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\). The hypograph of \(g\) relative to \(C\) is \[\operatorname{hypo}_C g=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}:t\le g(x)\}.\] The function \(g\) is concave on \(C\) if and only if \(\operatorname{hypo}_C g\) is convex. Consequently, an inequality \(t\le g(x)\) with concave \(g\) is a convex lower-graph constraint in the lifted variables \((x,t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hypograph consists of points lying on or below a function’s graph. A function is concave exactly when its hypograph is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex.
\(g:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\text{ is concave}\iff\operatorname{hypo}_C g\text{ is convex}.\)

notation.meaning: Hypograph of g relative to C.

children.title: Strict Graph Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Boundary behavior associated with strict graph inequalities and unattained limiting points.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Graph Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict epigraph and hypograph sets obtained by excluding graph equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a function \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), its strict epigraph and strict hypograph are respectively \[\operatorname{epi}^{<}f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)<t\},\qquad \operatorname{hypo}^{<}f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:t<f(x)\}.\] At every \(x\) where \(f(x)\) is finite, the equality point \((x,f(x))\) belongs to neither strict set. Thus strict graph inequalities omit the graph boundary retained by the non-strict epigraph or hypograph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict epigraph and hypograph inequalities exclude equality points on the function graph, unlike their non-strict counterparts.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty set.
\(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,f(x))\notin\operatorname{epi}^{<}f\cup\operatorname{hypo}^{<}f\) whenever \(f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\).

source_refs.locator: 2 Convex Analysis on Symmetric Matrices p. 13

children.title: Open Graph Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Topological openness in graph representations and its effect on representable feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Open Graph Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semicontinuity characterization through openness of strict graph sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological space and give \(X\times\mathbb{R}\) the product topology. For \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), the strict epigraph \(\{(x,t):f(x)<t\}\) is open if and only if \(f\) is upper semicontinuous. Dually, the strict hypograph \(\{(x,t):t<f(x)\}\) is open if and only if \(f\) is lower semicontinuous. Openness therefore depends on the semicontinuity direction opposite to that governing closed non-strict graph sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict epigraph is open exactly for an upper-semicontinuous function; a strict hypograph is open exactly for a lower-semicontinuous function.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space.
\(X\times\mathbb{R}\) has the product topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}^{<}f\text{ open}\iff f\text{ upper semicontinuous}\), and \(\operatorname{hypo}^{<}f\text{ open}\iff f\text{ lower semicontinuous}.\)
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the topological semicontinuity equivalences.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated semicontinuity equivalences are mathematically standard and match the leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator supports these nontrivial topological claims.

children.title: Closed Graph Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Closed graph representations, closure behavior, and attainment-sensitive modeling.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Graph Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semicontinuity characterization through closed non-strict graph sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological space, give \(X\times\mathbb{R}\) the product topology, and let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). The epigraph \(\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)\le t\}\) is closed if and only if \(f\) is lower semicontinuous. Dually, the hypograph \(\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:t\le f(x)\}\) is closed if and only if \(f\) is upper semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A non-strict epigraph is closed exactly when the function is lower semicontinuous; a non-strict hypograph is closed exactly when the function is upper semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space.
\(X\times\mathbb{R}\) has the product topology.
\(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed}\iff f\text{ is lower semicontinuous}\), and \(\operatorname{hypo}f\text{ is closed}\iff f\text{ is upper semicontinuous}.\)

children.title: Boundary Closure Transitions
children.top_down_role: Structural changes produced when strict or open graph regions are replaced by their closures.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Closure Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of closed graph sets by closing their strict counterparts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological space. If \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed, then \[\overline{\operatorname{epi}^{<}f}=\operatorname{epi}f.\] Indeed, every finite boundary point \((x,f(x))\) is approached by \((x,f(x)+1/k)\). Dually, if \(\operatorname{hypo}f\) is closed, then \[\overline{\operatorname{hypo}^{<}f}=\operatorname{hypo}f,\] with boundary approached by \((x,f(x)-1/k)\). Without closedness, the closure may additionally contain limit points corresponding to the appropriate semicontinuous envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a strict epigraph or hypograph recovers its non-strict counterpart when that counterpart is closed; otherwise additional limiting boundary points may appear.
assumptions_latex: \(X\times\mathbb{R}\) carries the product topology.
\(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f\text{ closed}\Rightarrow\overline{\operatorname{epi}^{<}f}=\operatorname{epi}f\), with the dual hypograph statement.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports strict-to-closed graph transitions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict-to-nonstrict closure equalities are standard under the stated closedness assumptions, but no source is supplied. The record also contains proof-like approach sequences and an imprecise claim about an 'appropriate semicontinuous envelope'; these require correction after sourcing.

children.title: Convex-Minimization Objective Lifts
children.top_down_role: Objective lifts preserving convex minimization structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Minimization Objective Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph reformulation of a proper convex minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex, where properness means that \(f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\) for at least one \(x\in C\). Then \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}}\{t:f(x)\le t\}.\] If either problem attains its optimum, the optimal solutions of the original problem are exactly the projections onto \(x\) of the lifted optimal solutions, and every lifted optimum satisfies \(t=f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a proper convex function is equivalent to minimizing a real epigraph variable. The optimal value is preserved, and attained optimizers are recovered by projecting the lifted optimizers onto the original variable.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex.
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf\{t:(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R},\ f(x)\le t\}.\)

children.title: Upper-Graph Constraint Lifts

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Graph Constraint Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact auxiliary representation of an upper bound on a convex expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex, and let \(u:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be affine. The constraint \(f(x)\le u(x)\) admits the exact lift \[\exists t\in\mathbb{R}:\quad f(x)\le t,\qquad t\le u(x).\] Eliminating \(t\) recovers the original inequality, while both lifted inequalities define convex sets. More generally, \(u\) may be concave because \(t-u(x)\le0\) remains convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper bound on a convex expression can be split through an auxiliary epigraph variable without changing the feasible x-set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex.
\(f\) is convex and \(u\) is affine or concave on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\le u(x)\iff\exists t\in\mathbb{R}:f(x)\le t\le u(x).\)

children.title: Exact Graph Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Graph Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness defined by equality after eliminating all auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,m\in\mathbb{N}_0\), let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a target graph-derived set, and let \(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\) be a lifted set with original variable \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and auxiliary variable \(z\in\mathbb{R}^m\). The lift \(L\) is an exact representation of \(S\) when \[S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ (x,z)\in L\}.\] Equivalently, exactness consists of soundness, \((x,z)\in L\Rightarrow x\in S\), and completeness, \(x\in S\Rightarrow\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^m\text{ such that }(x,z)\in L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted graph representation is exact when eliminating its auxiliary variables yields precisely the intended original set. Every lifted feasible point must project into the target set, and every target point must have an auxiliary witness.
assumptions_latex: \(n,m\in\mathbb{N}_0\).
\(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ (x,z)\in L\}.\)

notation.meaning: Target set in the original variables.
Original variable in the target space.

children.title: Lifted-Set Projection
children.top_down_role: Projection of lifted feasible geometry onto the original variable space.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted-Set Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate projection as the formal elimination map for lifted feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Z\) be nonempty sets, let \(L\subseteq X\times Z\), and define the coordinate projection \(\pi_X:X\times Z\to X\) by \(\pi_X(x,z)=x\). Then \[\pi_X(L)=\{x\in X:\exists z\in Z,\ (x,z)\in L\}.\] If \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(Z=\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(L\) is convex, then \(\pi_X(L)\) is convex. Even with the usual Euclidean topologies, a closed convex set \(L\) can have a projection \(\pi_X(L)\) that is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate projection eliminates auxiliary variables existentially. In finite-dimensional real vector spaces it preserves convexity, but it need not preserve closedness, even for closed convex lifted sets.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Z\) are nonempty sets.
\(L\subseteq X\times Z\).
For the convexity and closedness claims, \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Z=\mathbb{R}^m\) with their usual Euclidean structures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_X(L)=\{x\in X:\exists z\in Z,\ (x,z)\in L\}\), and in Euclidean spaces \(L\text{ convex}\Rightarrow\pi_X(L)\text{ convex}.\)

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Elimination
children.top_down_role: Structural removal of introduced variables from graph representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination is existential quantification over the auxiliary coordinates of a lifted feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces and let \(L\subseteq X\times Y\) be a lifted feasible set. Eliminating the auxiliary variable \(y\) means replacing \((x,y)\in L\) by the predicate
\[x\in E_L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y\in Y\text{ such that }(x,y)\in L.\]
Thus \(E_L=\operatorname{proj}_X L\). For a lifted optimization problem whose objective is \(f(x)\), elimination produces \(\inf\{f(x):x\in E_L\}\); no minimization over \(y\) appears in the objective unless the original lifted objective depends on \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary-variable elimination existentially quantifies the hidden coordinates, yielding exactly the projection of the lifted feasible set onto the original variables.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(L\subseteq X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_L=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ (x,y)\in L\}=\operatorname{proj}_X L\).

notation.meaning: set obtained after eliminating auxiliary variables

children.title: Projection Exactness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which projected lifted geometry differs from the intended original geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Exactness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes exact recovery and the two one-sided failures of a lifted feasible representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\subseteq X\) be the intended feasible set and \(L\subseteq X\times Y\) a proposed lift. Projection is exact precisely when every intended feasible point has a lifted witness and no unintended point has one:
\[\bigl(\forall x\in F\;\exists y\in Y:(x,y)\in L\bigr)\quad\text{and}\quad\bigl(\forall(x,y)\in L:x\in F\bigr).\]
Equivalently, \(\operatorname{proj}_X L=F\). Failure of the first condition removes feasible points; failure of the second introduces spurious feasible points. Neither inclusion alone establishes exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lift is projection-exact exactly when every original feasible point has a witness and every lifted point projects to an original feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_X L=F\) if and only if \(F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_X L\) and \(\operatorname{proj}_X L\subseteq F\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically correct and exactly characterizes projection exactness, including its two one-sided failures. However, no inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: Optimization Outcome Recovery Interface
children.top_down_role: Recovery of original model outcomes from lifted solutions.

children.title: Optimal-Value Recovery
children.top_down_role: Mapping solver-facing objective outcomes back to the original model value.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Value Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value preservation for an exact lift whose objective depends only on original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\subseteq X\), \(L\subseteq X\times Y\), and let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). Define
\[p=\inf_{x\in F}f(x),\qquad p_L=\inf_{(x,y)\in L}f(x).\]
If \(\operatorname{proj}_X L=F\), then \(p_L=p\), including the extended values \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\). More generally, \(\operatorname{proj}_X L\supseteq F\) implies \(p_L\le p\), whereas \(\operatorname{proj}_X L\subseteq F\) implies \(p_L\ge p\). These conclusions require the lifted objective to equal \(f(x)\) on every lifted point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact projection preserves the infimum. Outer projected approximations give lower bounds, while inner projected approximations give upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
The lifted objective at \((x,y)\) is \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_X L=F\Longrightarrow p_L=p\).

children.title: Optimizer Recovery
children.top_down_role: Mapping lifted solution variables back to original-model optimizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projects lifted minimizers to original minimizers and characterizes which original minimizers admit lifted representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\subseteq X\), \(L\subseteq X\times Y\), and \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), with \(\operatorname{proj}_X L=F\). If the lifted objective is \(f(x)\), then
\[\operatorname{proj}_X\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x,y)\in L}f(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x).\]
Consequently, every lifted optimizer projects to an original optimizer, and every original optimizer has at least one auxiliary witness that forms a lifted optimizer. The equality remains valid when both argmin sets are empty; it asserts no uniqueness of either the projected optimizer or its witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under exact projection and an unchanged objective, projecting all lifted minimizers gives exactly all original minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_X L=F\).
The lifted objective at \((x,y)\) is \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_X\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x,y)\in L}f(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct argmin correspondence under exact projection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The argmin projection identity is correct under exact projection and an objective depending only on the original variable, including the empty-argmin case. No authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Recovery Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Nonuniqueness, missing auxiliary information, or projection effects that limit outcome recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Recovery Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates ambiguity of auxiliary witnesses from nonuniqueness of the recovered original optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L\subseteq X\times Y\), define the fiber \(L_x=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in L\}\). Even when \(\operatorname{proj}_X L=F\) and optimizer recovery is exact, a recovered optimizer \(x^\star\) need not determine a unique lifted optimizer: ambiguity occurs whenever \(|L_{x^\star}|>1\). Conversely, uniqueness of a lifted optimizer implies uniqueness of its projection, but uniqueness of \(x^\star\) does not imply uniqueness of its auxiliary witness. A single-valued recovery map exists on a set \(S\subseteq F\) only after selecting one element from every nonempty fiber \(L_x\), and it is canonical only with additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact recovery does not make auxiliary witnesses unique; a unique original optimizer may correspond to many lifted optimizers in its fiber.
assumptions_latex: \(L\subseteq X\times Y\).
\(x^\star\in\operatorname{proj}_X L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|L_{x^\star}|>1\Longrightarrow\) the auxiliary recovery of \(x^\star\) is nonunique.

notation.meaning: auxiliary fiber over the point x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fiber-based distinction between optimizer nonuniqueness and auxiliary-witness nonuniqueness is correct and fits a failure-boundary container. The record needs an authoritative source for recovery multifunctions, selections, or lift fibers.

children.title: Inexact Graph Substitution Regimes
children.top_down_role: Graph substitutions that yield bounds or approximations rather than exact equivalence.

children.title: Relaxing Graph Substitutions
children.top_down_role: Graph replacements that enlarge or otherwise relax the represented feasible geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxing Graph Substitutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a relaxation by outer containment of the exact lifted graph or feasible representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\subseteq X\times Y\) encode an exact graph-based constraint and let \(\widetilde G\subseteq X\times Y\) replace it. The substitution is relaxing when
\[G\subseteq\widetilde G.\]
If all other constraints are unchanged, the corresponding exact and substituted lifted feasible sets satisfy \(L\subseteq\widetilde L\), hence \(\operatorname{proj}_X L\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_X\widetilde L\). For minimization with the same objective \(f(x)\), the relaxed optimal value cannot exceed the exact value. Equality of values or optimizers is not implied by containment and requires an additional tightness argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxing substitution replaces an exact graph constraint by an outer set, enlarging feasibility and producing a lower bound in minimization.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and \(\widetilde G\) are substituted within otherwise identical constraints.
The optimization objective is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\subseteq\widetilde G\Longrightarrow\operatorname{proj}_X L\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_X\widetilde L\).

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Robust Counterpart representation of a safe convex approximation to a scalar chance constraint p. 111

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Robust Counterpart representation of a safe convex approximation to a scalar chance constraint p. 111

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The outer-containment definition and its minimization consequence are correct for direct replacement of an otherwise unchanged membership constraint. The cited safe approximation of a chance constraint is example-specific and may describe an inner restriction rather than the outer relaxation defined here.

children.title: Approximating Graph Substitutions
children.top_down_role: Finite or surrogate graph representations used in place of exact graph geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximating Graph Substitutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines quantitative graph approximation through two-sided set enlargement in a specified metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((Z,d)\) be a metric space, let \(G\subseteq Z\) be an exact graph representation, and let \(\widetilde G\subseteq Z\) be its substitute. For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), call \(\widetilde G\) an \(\varepsilon\)-approximation of \(G\) when
\[G\subseteq(\widetilde G)_\varepsilon\quad\text{and}\quad\widetilde G\subseteq(G)_\varepsilon,\qquad S_\varepsilon=\{z\in Z:d(z,S)\le\varepsilon\}.\]
Equivalently, the Hausdorff distance is at most \(\varepsilon\) when the relevant sets are nonempty and that distance is finite. This geometric approximation alone gives no objective-value error bound without regularity connecting objective variation and feasibility perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximating substitution lies within a prescribed two-sided metric tolerance of the exact graph; value accuracy additionally requires stability assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \((Z,d)\) is a metric space.
\(G\) and \(\widetilde G\) are nonempty graph representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm H}(G,\widetilde G)\le\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-sided neighborhood condition is a valid Hausdorff-distance formulation for nonempty sets, and the definition fits the container. The selected metric convention and the stated limitation on value accuracy need an authoritative source.

children.title: Bound Direction
children.top_down_role: The upper-bound or lower-bound interpretation induced by an inexact substitution.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound Direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tracks minimization and maximization bounds induced by inner or outer projected feasible approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq F\subseteq F_{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq X\), and let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). For minimization,
\[\inf_{x\in F_{\mathrm{out}}}f(x)\le\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\le\inf_{x\in F_{\mathrm{in}}}f(x).\]
For maximization, both inequalities reverse:
\[\sup_{x\in F_{\mathrm{in}}}f(x)\le\sup_{x\in F}f(x)\le\sup_{x\in F_{\mathrm{out}}}f(x).\]
Thus an outer relaxation supplies a lower bound for a minimization problem and an upper bound for a maximization problem; an inner restriction supplies the opposite bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer feasible approximations lower minimization values and raise maximization values; inner approximations produce the opposite bound directions.
assumptions_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq F\subseteq F_{\mathrm{out}}\).
All problems use the same extended-real objective \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{F_{\mathrm{out}}}f\le\inf_F f\le\inf_{F_{\mathrm{in}}}f\), with reversed directions for suprema.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Robust Counterpart representation of a safe convex approximation to a scalar chance constraint p. 111

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Robust Counterpart representation of a safe convex approximation to a scalar chance constraint p. 111

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound directions for inner and outer feasible approximations are mathematically correct for the same objective. The cited safe-approximation section appears to support at most one minimization-side instance, not the full minimization/maximization and inner/outer statement.

children.title: Approximation Fidelity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where substitution error changes feasibility, objective quality, or recoverability.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Fidelity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies why small graph-set error alone need not control optimal values or optimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Hausdorff closeness of feasible representations does not by itself guarantee objective-value fidelity. For \(\varepsilon>0\), take \(F=\{0\}\), \(F_\varepsilon=\{\varepsilon\}\subset\mathbb R\), and \(f_M(x)=Mx\). Then \(d_{\mathrm H}(F,F_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\), but
\[\left|\inf_{x\in F_\varepsilon}f_M(x)-\inf_{x\in F}f_M(x)\right|=M\varepsilon,\]
which is unbounded over \(M\). A uniform value-error estimate therefore requires quantitative objective regularity, such as a fixed Lipschitz constant, together with a perturbation measure that controls the projected feasible sets. Optimizer-distance bounds generally require additional growth or uniqueness conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily close feasible sets can have arbitrarily different values when objective sensitivity is uncontrolled; optimizer accuracy requires still stronger stability.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(M>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm H}(F,F_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\) while the value error equals \(M\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct and demonstrates that Hausdorff closeness alone gives no value-error bound uniform over objective sensitivity. The broader claims about value and optimizer stability require an authoritative perturbation-analysis source.

children.title: Indicator-Function Graphs
children.top_down_role: Extended-value graph encodings of feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator-Function Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encodes membership in a feasible set through an extended-real convex function and its epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a set \(C\subseteq X\), its indicator function is
\[\delta_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\]
Consequently, \(x\in C\) if and only if \(\delta_C(x)\le0\), and
\[\operatorname{epi}\delta_C=C\times[0,+\infty).\]
The function \(\delta_C\) is proper exactly when \(C\ne\varnothing\), convex exactly when \(C\) is convex, and lower semicontinuous exactly when \(C\) is closed. Thus closed convex feasible sets correspond to proper lower-semicontinuous convex indicator functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is encoded by a function equal to zero on the set and positive infinity outside; its epigraph is the set times the nonnegative ray.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\), where \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\delta_C=C\times[0,+\infty)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The indicator-function representation, epigraph identity, and properness, convexity, and lower-semicontinuity correspondences are correct in the stated finite-dimensional setting. The representation kind fits the topic, but no authoritative convex-analysis citation is supplied.

children.title: Partial-Minimization Value Graphs
children.top_down_role: Convex value functions represented through hidden minimizing variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Minimization Value Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a convex value function by eliminating hidden variables from a jointly convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper and convex, and define
\[g(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y).\]
Then \(g\) is convex whenever it never takes \(-\infty\). Its strict epigraph satisfies the exact projection identity
\[\{(x,t):g(x)<t\}=\operatorname{proj}_{X\times\mathbb R}\{(x,y,t):F(x,y)<t\}.\]
Moreover, \(\operatorname{epi}g\) equals the corresponding projection of \(\operatorname{epi}F\) when the infimum is attained for every \(x\) with finite \(g(x)\); without attainment, the projected epigraph can omit boundary points and closure may be necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization yields a convex value function. Its strict epigraph is always a projection; its closed epigraph needs attainment or closure.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is proper and jointly convex.
\(g(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=\inf_y F(x,y)\) is convex and its strict epigraph is the displayed projection.

source_refs.locator: 3.3. Partial Minimization of Convex Functions p. 122

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3. Partial Minimization of Convex Functions p. 122

children.title: Partial-Maximization Value Graphs
children.top_down_role: Concave value functions represented through hidden maximizing variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Maximization Value Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a concave value function by eliminating hidden variables from a jointly concave function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper and concave, and define
\[h(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}H(x,y).\]
Then \(h\) is concave whenever it never takes \(+\infty\). Its strict hypograph satisfies
\[\{(x,t):t<h(x)\}=\operatorname{proj}_{X\times\mathbb R}\{(x,y,t):t<H(x,y)\}.\]
Moreover, \(\operatorname{hypo}h\) equals the projection of \(\operatorname{hypo}H\) when the supremum is attained for every \(x\) with finite \(h(x)\); otherwise projected hypographs can omit boundary points. This is the sign-reversed counterpart of partial minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial maximization yields a concave value function. Its strict hypograph is always a projection; boundary recovery needs attainment or closure.
assumptions_latex: \(H:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is proper and jointly concave.
\(h(x)<+\infty\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(x)=\sup_y H(x,y)\) is concave and its strict hypograph is the displayed projection.

source_refs.locator: 3.3. Partial Minimization of Convex Functions p. 122

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3. Partial Minimization of Convex Functions p. 122

children.title: Implicit-Domain Graphs
children.top_down_role: Domain information carried by extended-value atoms and graph implementations.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is an extended-real-valued function on a real vector space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ f(x)\le r\}\).

notation.meaning: Effective domain of the extended-value atom.
Epigraph used as the graph implementation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended values encode domain constraints directly in an epigraph implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The epigraph implementation of \(f\) is
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le r\}.\]
Because the inequality is false when \(f(x)=+\infty\), this set equals
\[\{(x,r):x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ f(x)\le r\}.\]
Thus membership in the implemented graph simultaneously imposes the atom inequality and the implicit constraint \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\); no separate domain constraint is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-value atom’s epigraph automatically enforces its effective domain: points assigned positive infinity cannot belong to the graph implementation.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-Domain Graphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically standard and fits the Implicit-Domain Graphs container, but no inspectable citation or locator supports the extended-value epigraph claim.

children.title: Scale-Structured Graph Lift Family
children.top_down_role: Graph lifts organized by scaling, homogenization, and positive-domain perspective structure.

children.title: Scalar Perspective Graphs
children.top_down_role: Graph families obtained from scalar perspective transformations.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper function on a real vector space \(X\).
The scale satisfies \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\ge t f(x/t)\iff (x/t,r/t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\).

notation.meaning: Positive-scale perspective of the scalar-valued atom.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-scale scalar perspective; the zero-scale closure is treated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), define the scalar perspective by \(p_f(x,t)=t f(x/t)\). Its epigraph admits the scaled graph representation
\[\operatorname{epi}p_f\cap\{t>0\}=\{(x,t,r):t>0,\ (x/t,r/t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\]
Equivalently,
\[r\ge t f(x/t)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x/t)\le r/t.\]
If \(f\) is convex, then \(p_f\) is convex on its positive-scale domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At positive scale, a perspective epigraph is obtained by multiplying every coordinate of the original epigraph by the same scalar.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Perspective Graphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-scale perspective representation and content kind fit the container, but the record supplies no source or specific locator.

children.title: Homogeneous Gauge Lift Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Lifted graph forms organized by positive homogeneity and gauge structure.

children.title: Homogeneous Graph Lifts
children.top_down_role: Lifted graph forms organized by positive scaling structure.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(E=\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq X\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_f=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\{(x,1,r):(x,r)\in E\}\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic homogenization of a closed convex epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The homogeneous graph lift of \(f\) is
\[K_f=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\{(x,1,r)\in X\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R:(x,r)\in E\}.\]
It is a closed convex cone and its unit-scale slice recovers the original graph implementation:
\[E=\{(x,r):(x,1,r)\in K_f\}.\]
For every \(t>0\), its scale-\(t\) slice satisfies
\[(x,t,r)\in K_f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\ge t f(x/t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing the conic hull of an epigraph embedded at unit scale produces a homogeneous cone whose unit slice recovers that epigraph.
knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Graph Lifts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The homogenized epigraph construction fits the container, but closure and lower semicontinuity require a specified topology or finite-dimensional setting. An authoritative source is needed to establish the intended hypotheses and slice identities.

children.title: Gauge Graph Lifts
children.top_down_role: Lifted representations organized around gauge-valued expressions and gauge sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, with \(0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma_C=\{(x,t):t>0,\ x\in tC\}\cup\bigl(\operatorname{rec}C\times\{0\}\bigr)\).

notation.meaning: Minkowski gauge generated by the set.
Recession cone of the generating set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed epigraph lift of a gauge, including its zero-scale recession slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the gauge by
\[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\ge0:x\in tC\},\]
with the infimum of the empty set equal to \(+\infty\). Its closed graph lift is
\[\operatorname{epi}\gamma_C=\{(x,t):t>0,\ x\in tC\}\cup\bigl(\operatorname{rec}C\times\{0\}\bigr).\]
Equivalently,
\[\operatorname{epi}\gamma_C=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,t):t>0,\ x\in tC\}.\]
The unit-scale slice is \(C\), namely \(C=\{x:(x,1)\in\operatorname{epi}\gamma_C\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge epigraph is the closed homogenization of its unit sublevel set; its zero-scale slice is the set’s recession cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Graph Lifts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gauge epigraph and recession-slice representation fits the container, but closedness and recession terminology require a specified topological setting, and no supporting source is cited.

children.title: Scaling Degeneracy Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Zero-scale, sign, or domain regimes that disrupt homogeneous or gauge representations.

assumptions_latex: \(C=[-1,+\infty)\subset\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(x,t):t>0,\ x\in tC\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\) is not closed.

notation.meaning: Positive-scale homogenization with only the origin inserted at zero scale.
Recession cone of the example set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of naive zero-scale homogenization for an unbounded generating set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[H=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2:t>0,\ x\in tC\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.\]
Since \(tC=[-t,+\infty)\), every \((x,0)\) with \(x>0\) is the limit of \((x,t_k)\in H\) for any sequence \(t_k\downarrow0\), but \((x,0)\notin H\). Hence \(H\) is not closed. Its closure adds exactly the missing recession slice \(\operatorname{rec}C\times\{0\}=[0,+\infty)\times\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an unbounded set, adding only the origin at zero scale can leave the homogenized graph nonclosed; the full recession slice is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Degeneracy Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct and failure_boundary is the appropriate kind, but the record lacks an inspectable source and locator.

children.title: Perspective Domain Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Closure and limiting-value regimes at the scaling boundary.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(f^\infty\) denotes the recession function of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline p_f(x,t)=t f(x/t)\) for \(t>0\), \(\overline p_f(x,0)=f^\infty(x)\), and \(\overline p_f(x,t)=+\infty\) for \(t<0\).

notation.meaning: Recession function of the base function.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex extension of the perspective across the zero-scale boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed perspective is the extended-value function
\[\overline p_f(x,t)=\begin{cases}t f(x/t),&t>0,\\ f^\infty(x),&t=0,\\ +\infty,&t<0.\end{cases}\]
Its epigraph is the closure of the positive-scale perspective epigraph:
\[\operatorname{epi}\overline p_f=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,t,r):t>0,\ r\ge t f(x/t)\}.\]
Thus the admissible limiting values at \(t=0\) are exactly those satisfying \(r\ge f^\infty(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective uses the recession function at zero scale and positive infinity at negative scales, making the positive-scale epigraph closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Perspective Domain Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated zero-scale recession extension is standard and matches the boundary container, but closure, lower semicontinuity, and the recession function need an explicit finite-dimensional or topological setting supported by a cited source.

children.title: Absolute-Value Graphs
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral graph templates for scalar or componentwise absolute-value atoms.

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute-Value Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral epigraph template for the scalar absolute value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The absolute-value epigraph has the exact polyhedral representation
\[\operatorname{epi}|\cdot|=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^2:r\ge x,\ r\ge -x\}.\]
Thus
\[r\ge |x|\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\ge x\ \text{and}\ r\ge -x.\]
For each fixed \(x\in\mathbb R\), the smallest feasible graph variable is
\[\min\{r\in\mathbb R:r\ge x,\ r\ge -x\}=|x|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The absolute-value epigraph is the intersection of the halfspaces defined by r at least x and r at least minus x; for fixed x, the smallest feasible r equals |x|.
assumptions_latex: \(x,r\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\ge |x|\iff r\ge x\ \text{and}\ r\ge -x\).

children.title: Positive-Part Graphs
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral graph templates for positive-part atoms.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Part Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral epigraph template for the scalar positive-part function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \((x)_+=\max\{x,0\}\), the epigraph is
\[\operatorname{epi}(\cdot)_+=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^2:r\ge x,\ r\ge0\}.\]
Thus
\[r\ge(x)_+\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\ge x\ \text{and}\ r\ge0.\]
For each fixed \(x\in\mathbb R\), the smallest feasible graph variable is
\[\min\{r\in\mathbb R:r\ge x,\ r\ge0\}=(x)_+.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive-part epigraph is defined by the affine lower bounds r at least x and r at least zero; for fixed x, the smallest feasible r is the positive part of x.
assumptions_latex: \(x,r\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\ge (x)_+\iff r\ge x\ \text{and}\ r\ge0\).

children.title: Hinge Graphs
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral graph templates for shifted one-sided hinge atoms.

knowledge_statements.title: Hinge Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine scalar hinge represented by a two-halfspace epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the affine hinge \(h(x)=\max\{0,a+bx\}\),
\[\operatorname{epi}h=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^2:r\ge0,\ r\ge a+bx\}.\]
Equivalently,
\[r\ge h(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\ge0\ \text{and}\ r\ge a+bx.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine hinge is the maximum of zero and an affine expression, so its epigraph is defined by those two affine lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(a,b,x,r\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\ge\max\{0,a+bx\}\iff r\ge0\ \text{and}\ r\ge a+bx\).

children.title: Finite Extremum Graph Duality
children.top_down_role: Epigraph and hypograph templates for finite pointwise extrema.

children.title: Finite-Maximum Graphs
children.top_down_role: Graph templates for finite pointwise maxima of supported expressions.

assumptions_latex: \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where \(m\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(\max_i f_i)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{epi}f_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph intersection rule for a finite pointwise maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(F(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\). Then
\[\operatorname{epi}F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{epi}f_i,\]
because
\[r\ge F(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\ge f_i(x)\ \text{for every }i.\]
Hence a graph implementation of the finite maximum shares one epigraph variable \(r\) among the component inequalities. If every \(f_i\) is convex, then \(F\) and its epigraph are convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a finite maximum is the intersection of the component epigraphs, using one shared upper graph variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Maximum Graphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-maximum epigraph intersection rule is correct, complete, and appropriately classified as a representation, but it has no citation or locator.

children.title: Finite-Minimum Graphs
children.top_down_role: Graph templates for finite pointwise minima of supported expressions.

assumptions_latex: \(f_i:X\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where \(m\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{hypo}(\min_i f_i)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{hypo}f_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypograph intersection rule for a finite pointwise minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(G(x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\). Then
\[\operatorname{hypo}G=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{hypo}f_i,\]
because
\[r\le G(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\le f_i(x)\ \text{for every }i.\]
Hence a graph implementation of the finite minimum shares one hypograph variable \(r\) among the component inequalities. If every \(f_i\) is concave, then \(G\) and its hypograph are convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hypograph of a finite minimum is the intersection of the component hypographs, using one shared lower graph variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Minimum Graphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-minimum hypograph intersection rule is correct and fits the container, but no inspectable source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Extremum Orientation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Curvature and optimization-orientation limits governing finite-extremum graph use.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremum Orientation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp orientation distinction between maximum epigraphs and minimum hypographs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the affine functions \(f_1(x)=x\) and \(f_2(x)=-x\) on \(\mathbb R\),
\[\max\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}=|x|,\qquad \min\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}=-|x|.\]
The epigraph of \(|x|\) and the hypograph of \(-|x|\) are convex, whereas the hypograph of \(|x|\) and the epigraph of \(-|x|\) are nonconvex. Therefore finite maxima have the convex epigraph orientation and finite minima have the concave hypograph orientation; reversing these orientations can produce nonconvex graph sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum and minimum templates have opposite orientations: convex maxima use epigraphs and concave minima use hypographs, while reversing those orientations can produce nonconvex sets.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1(x)=x\) and \(f_2(x)=-x\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}=|x|\) and \(\min\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}=-|x|\); their reversed hypograph and epigraph orientations, respectively, are nonconvex and therefore show that reversed extremum orientations can fail.

notation.meaning: Pointwise maximum of the two affine functions.
Pointwise minimum of the two affine functions.

children.title: Piecewise-Affine Graphs
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral graph forms for convex and concave piecewise-affine atoms.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Affine Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex maxima and concave minima of affine functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a_i,c_j\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(b_i,d_j\in\mathbb{R}\). For \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^\top x+b_i)\) and \(g(x)=\min_{1\le j\le r}(c_j^\top x+d_j)\), their canonical one-sided graph representations are
\[\operatorname{epi} f=\{(x,t):a_i^\top x+b_i\le t\ \text{for all }i\},\qquad \operatorname{hypo} g=\{(x,t):t\le c_j^\top x+d_j\ \text{for all }j\}.\]
Thus both sets are polyhedra, and equality graphs are their respective lower or upper boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite affine maximum has a polyhedral epigraph, while a finite affine minimum has a polyhedral hypograph, each described by one inequality per affine piece.
assumptions_latex: \(m,r\in\mathbb{N}\) are finite.
\(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f\) and \(\operatorname{hypo}g\) admit finite linear-inequality descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordered-Statistic Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-union representation of the decreasing rearrangement map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(x_{[1]}\ge\cdots\ge x_{[n]}\) denote its components in nonincreasing order and set \(s(x)=(x_{[1]},\ldots,x_{[n]})\). Then
\[\operatorname{gph}s=\bigcup_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_n}\{(x,y):x_{\pi(1)}\ge\cdots\ge x_{\pi(n)},\ y_i=x_{\pi(i)}\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,n\}.\]
Every member of the union is polyhedral. When components tie, multiple permutation pieces describe the same ordered value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sorting-map graph is a finite union of polyhedra, one for each permutation; ties cause several pieces to overlap.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\).
\(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}s\) is a finite union of permutation-indexed polyhedra.

children.title: Top-k Graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Top-k Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph of the vector containing the largest \(k\) components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and define \(T_k(x)=(x_{[1]},\ldots,x_{[k]})\). Its graph has the exact disjunctive representation
\[\operatorname{gph}T_k=\bigcup_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_n}\{(x,y):x_{\pi(1)}\ge\cdots\ge x_{\pi(n)},\ y_i=x_{\pi(i)}\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,k\}.\]
Consequently, the top-\(k\) vector graph is generally nonconvex but is a finite union of polyhedra; coincident component values produce overlapping pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordered top-k vector has a permutation-indexed finite-union graph. It is generally nonconvex, with overlapping polyhedral pieces at ties.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(1\le k\le n\).
\(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}T_k\) is a finite union of polyhedra.

children.title: Sum-of-Largest Graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Sum-of-Largest Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral epigraph of the sum of the \(k\) largest components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \(S_k(x)=\sum_{i=1}^k x_{[i]}\). Then
\[S_k(x)=\max\Bigl\{\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i:0\le w_i\le1,\ \sum_{i=1}^n w_i=k\Bigr\}=\min_{\tau\in\mathbb{R}}\Bigl(k\tau+\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\tau)_+\Bigr).\]
Hence
\[\operatorname{epi}S_k=\{(x,t):\exists\tau,u,\ u_i\ge x_i-\tau,\ u_i\ge0,\ k\tau+\sum_i u_i\le t\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of the k largest components is convex and has an exact linear extended epigraph using one threshold and nonnegative excess variables.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(1\le k\le n\).
\(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}S_k\) is the projection of the displayed polyhedron.

notation.meaning: sum of the k largest components

children.title: Tie-Regime Geometry

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Regime Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subdifferential geometry of a largest-\(k\) sum at ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S_k(x)=\sum_{i=1}^k x_{[i]}\) and let \(\theta=x_{[k]}\). Its subdifferential is
\[\partial S_k(x)=\left\{w\in[0,1]^n:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i=k,\ w_i=1\ \text{if }x_i>\theta,\ w_i=0\ \text{if }x_i<\theta\right\}.\]
Weights on the tie set \(\{i:x_i=\theta\}\) may vary subject to their required sum. Thus \(S_k\) is differentiable exactly when the admissible weight vector is unique; in particular, it is differentiable whenever \(x_{[k]}>x_{[k+1]}\), using \(x_{[n+1]}=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the selection threshold, tied components share fractional subgradient weights. A strict gap after the kth component yields a unique gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(1\le k\le n\) and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial S_k(x)\) is the displayed face of the capped simplex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exposed-face characterization of the capped-simplex support function

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral-Norm Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite linear epigraph model for norms with polyhedral unit balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}_+\) be a norm whose unit ball is a polytope. Then the dual unit ball has finitely many vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\), and
\[p(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}v_i^\top x,\qquad \operatorname{epi}p=\{(x,t):v_i^\top x\le t\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,m\}.\]
Conversely, if the displayed maximum is finite, symmetric, positive definite, and positively homogeneous, it defines a polyhedral norm with this epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm is polyhedral precisely when it is a finite maximum of linear functionals satisfying the norm axioms; its epigraph is given by linear inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
The unit ball of \(p\) is a polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}p\) has a finite linear-inequality representation.

children.title: Euclidean Norm Graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Norm Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone representation of the Euclidean-norm epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the Euclidean norm is \(\|x\|_2=(x^\top x)^{1/2}\). Its epigraph is exactly
\[\operatorname{epi}\|\cdot\|_2=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:\|x\|_2\le t\}=\mathcal{Q}_{n+1},\]
where \(\mathcal{Q}_{n+1}\) is the Lorentz cone. Therefore an inequality \(\|Ax+b\|_2\le c^\top x+d\) is represented by the affine conic membership \((c^\top x+d,Ax+b)\in\mathcal{Q}_{m+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Euclidean-norm epigraph is the Lorentz cone, so affine Euclidean-norm inequalities are second-order-cone constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(d\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|Ax+b\|_2\le c^\top x+d\iff(c^\top x+d,Ax+b)\in\mathcal{Q}_{m+1}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: defining Lorentz-cone representation of the Euclidean norm
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Lorentz-cone representation is correct and appropriately classified, but it lacks a source with a section, theorem, or page locator.

children.title: Ellipsoidal Norm Graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoidal Norm Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone graph for a positive-definite quadratic norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\) and choose a factor \(L\) satisfying \(Q=L^\top L\). The ellipsoidal norm \(p_Q(x)=(x^\top Qx)^{1/2}=\|Lx\|_2\) has epigraph
\[\operatorname{epi}p_Q=\{(x,t):(t,Lx)\in\mathcal{Q}_{n+1}\}.\]
Equivalently, \(p_Q(x)\le t\) is a second-order-cone constraint. Its unit ball \(\{x:x^\top Qx\le1\}\) is an ellipsoid because positive definiteness makes \(L\) injective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite quadratic norm becomes an ordinary Euclidean norm after factoring its matrix, yielding an exact second-order-cone epigraph.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\).
\(Q=L^\top L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_Q(x)\le t\iff(t,Lx)\in\mathcal{Q}_{n+1}\).

children.title: Singular-Transformation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Degenerate transformations that yield seminorm behavior or lower-dimensional geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Transformation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneration of transformed Euclidean norms under a singular map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be rank deficient and define \(p_L(x)=\|Lx\|_2\). The epigraph remains second-order-cone representable:
\[\operatorname{epi}p_L=\{(x,t):(t,Lx)\in\mathcal{Q}_{m+1}\}.\]
However, \(p_L\) is only a seminorm because
\[p_L(x)=0\iff x\in\ker L,\]
and \(\ker L\) contains a nonzero vector. Its unit sublevel set is unbounded along \(\ker L\); it becomes a genuine norm on the quotient space \(\mathbb{R}^n/\ker L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-deficient transformation preserves the conic epigraph but produces a seminorm, with an unbounded unit set along the transformation kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(L\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(\operatorname{rank}L<n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_L\) is not a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), although its epigraph is second-order-cone representable.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: null-space characterization of a transformed Euclidean seminorm

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Function Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted Euclidean-distance epigraph for a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed, and define \(d_C(x)=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|_2\). In finite dimensions the infimum is attained, and
\[\operatorname{epi}d_C=\{(x,t):\exists y\in C\ \text{such that }(t,x-y)\in\mathcal{Q}_{n+1}\}.\]
If \(C\) is convex, this is a convex lifted representation. If \(C\) itself has a conic representation, adjoining its constraints gives a conic formulation of the distance epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a nonempty closed set has a lifted norm epigraph. For a convex conically represented set, this yields a convex conic formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and closed.
The norm is \(\|\cdot\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}d_C\iff\exists y\in C:(t,x-y)\in\mathcal{Q}_{n+1}\).

children.title: Projection-Value Graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Value Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone characterization of Euclidean projection onto a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the projection \(P_C(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}\|x-z\|_2\) exists and is unique. Its graph satisfies
\[\operatorname{gph}P_C=\{(x,y):y\in C,\ x-y\in N_C(y)\},\]
where \(N_C(y)=\{v:v^\top(z-y)\le0\ \text{for every }z\in C\}\). Moreover, the optimal value obeys \(d_C(x)=\|x-P_C(x)\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a nonempty closed convex set is unique and is characterized by the residual belonging to the set's normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Distances use the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=P_C(x)\iff y\in C\ \text{and}\ x-y\in N_C(y)\).

notation.meaning: convex normal cone to C at y

children.title: Nearest-Point Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Regimes where a unique distance value corresponds to multiple projecting points.

knowledge_statements.title: Nearest-Point Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of projection uniqueness without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\{-1,1\}\subset\mathbb{R}\) and \(x=0\). The set \(C\) is nonempty and closed but not convex, and
\[d_C(0)=1,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}|0-y|=\{-1,1\}.\]
Thus the nearest-point map is set-valued at \(0\), even though the distance value is unique. Closedness guarantees attainment here but does not guarantee uniqueness; convexity of \(C\), together with the strictly convex squared Euclidean objective, restores uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the closed nonconvex set containing minus one and one, zero has two nearest points. Closedness alone therefore does not make projection single-valued.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\{-1,1\}\subset\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}|x-y|=\{-1,1\}\) is not a singleton.

knowledge_statements.title: Least-Squares Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotated second-order-cone epigraph of a finite-dimensional least-squares loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(f(x)=\|Ax-b\|_2^2\). For the rotated second-order cone \(\mathcal Q_r^{m+2}=\{(u,v,w):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\}\), the epigraph has the exact graph representation
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):(t,\tfrac12,Ax-b)\in\mathcal Q_r^{m+2}\}.\]
Thus canonicalizing a least-squares inequality requires one affine residual and one rotated-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A squared affine residual is bounded by t exactly when the residual and t form one rotated second-order-cone tuple.

\(b\in\mathbb R^m\)

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Quadratic Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotated-cone representation of a convex quadratic epigraph using a positive-semidefinite factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\), where \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), and choose \(R\in\mathbb R^{k\times n}\) satisfying \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\). Then
\[t\ge f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(t-q^{\mathsf T}x-r,1,Rx)\in\mathcal Q_r^{k+2},\]
where \(\mathcal Q_r^{k+2}=\{(u,v,w):u,v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\}\). The representation remains exact when \(Q\) is singular by taking \(k=\operatorname{rank}Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive-semidefinite quadratic epigraph is an affine slice of a rotated second-order cone, including rank-deficient quadratics.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\)
\(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\)
\(q\in\mathbb R^n,\ r\in\mathbb R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\iff(t-q^{\mathsf T}x-r,1,Rx)\in\mathcal Q_r^{k+2}\)

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nullspace behavior and reduced-rank canonicalization of a positive-semidefinite quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\) with \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\). For every \(z\in\ker Q\),
\[f(x+z)=f(x)+q^{\mathsf T}z.\]
Hence the quadratic curvature vanishes precisely along \(\ker Q\); if \(q\perp\ker Q\), the function and its epigraph are invariant under translations by \(\ker Q\). A rank factor \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\), with \(R\in\mathbb R^{k\times n}\) and \(k=\operatorname{rank}Q\), gives an exact reduced rotated-cone graph without requiring \(Q\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular positive-semidefinite quadratic has no curvature on its nullspace and admits an exact cone graph using only a rank-sized factor.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\)
\(z\in\ker Q\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x+z)=f(x)+q^{\mathsf T}z\)

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-over-Linear Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed perspective graph represented by one rotated second-order-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an affine residual \(w(x)=Ax+b\), define the closed quadratic-over-linear function
\[f(x,y)=\begin{cases}\|w(x)\|_2^2/y,&y>0,\\0,&y=0\text{ and }w(x)=0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
With \(\mathcal Q_r=\{(u,v,z):u,v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|z\|_2^2\}\), its epigraph is
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,y,t):(t,\tfrac y2,w(x))\in\mathcal Q_r\}.\]
The cone closure therefore handles the boundary \(y=0\) without a separate numerical division.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed quadratic-over-linear epigraph is exactly a rotated-cone constraint, including its zero-denominator boundary case.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\)
\(b\in\mathbb R^m\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge f(x,y)\iff(t,\tfrac y2,Ax+b)\in\mathcal Q_r\)

children.title: Scalar Power Graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Power Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-cone slices for convex epigraphs and nonnegative concave hypographs of scalar powers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(0<\alpha<1\), let
\[K_\alpha=\{(u,v,w):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ |w|\le u^\alpha v^{1-\alpha}\}.\]
If \(p>1\), the convex power epigraph satisfies
\[t\ge|x|^p\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(t,1,x)\in K_{1/p}.\]
If \(0<p<1\), the nonnegative portion of the concave power hypograph satisfies
\[x\ge0,\ t\ge0,\ t\le x^p\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(x,1,t)\in K_p.\]
Negative hypograph ordinates may be admitted separately because they automatically satisfy \(t\le x^p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar convex-power epigraphs and nonnegative concave-power hypographs are affine slices of suitable three-dimensional power cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge|x|^p\iff(t,1,x)\in K_{1/p}\) for \(p>1\), with the stated hypograph analogue for \(0<p<1\)

notation.meaning: Three-dimensional power cone with exponent alpha.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Geometric-Mean Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized power-cone hypograph of a weighted geometric mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a_i>0\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=1\), and define \(g(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i}\) on \(\mathbb R_+^n\). Its nonnegative hypograph is
\[\{(x,t):x\ge0,\ 0\le t\le g(x)\}=\{(x,t):x\ge0,\ |t|\le\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i},\ t\ge0\}.\]
Equivalently, \((x,t)\) belongs to the generalized power cone with weight vector \(a\). The full hypograph additionally contains every \((x,t)\) with \(x\ge0\) and \(t<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted geometric mean has a convex hypograph represented by a generalized power cone; negative ordinates are automatically feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R_+^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le t\le\prod_i x_i^{a_i}\iff |t|\le\prod_i x_i^{a_i}\text{ and }t\ge0\)

notation.meaning: Positive weight vector summing to one.

children.title: General p-Norm Graphs
children.top_down_role: Power-cone graph constructions for supported p-norm regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: General p-Norm Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-cone extended formulation of a finite-dimensional p-norm epigraph for p greater than one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p>1\), \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(K_{1/p}\) be the three-dimensional power cone. Then
\[t\ge\|x\|_p\]
holds exactly when \(t\ge0\) and there exist \(r_1,\ldots,r_n\ge0\) such that
\[\sum_{i=1}^n r_i\le t,\qquad(r_i,t,x_i)\in K_{1/p}\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).\]
Indeed, each cone constraint is equivalent to \(|x_i|^p\le r_i t^{p-1}\); their sum yields the norm inequality, and the converse follows by choosing \(r_i=|x_i|^p/t^{p-1}\) when \(t>0\), with \(t=0\) handled by closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A p-norm epigraph for p greater than one uses one auxiliary per coordinate and one power-cone constraint per coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge\|x\|_p\iff\exists r\ge0:\sum_i r_i\le t\text{ and }(r_i,t,x_i)\in K_{1/p}\)

children.title: Power-Cone Decomposition Graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Power-Cone Decomposition Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-tree decomposition of rational weighted geometric means into primitive three-dimensional power cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input positive rational weights \(a_i\) summing to one, variables \(x_i\ge0\), and a target \(t\ge0\). Build a rooted binary tree whose leaves are \(y_i=x_i\). For each internal node \(v\), let \(L_v\) and \(R_v\) be its child subtrees, set
\[\theta_v=\frac{\sum_{i\in L_v}a_i}{\sum_{i\in L_v\cup R_v}a_i},\]
and introduce \(y_v\ge0\) constrained by \((y_{L_v},y_{R_v},y_v)\in K_{\theta_v}\). Stop after processing the root and impose \(t\le y_{\mathrm{root}}\). The resulting primitive-cone system projects exactly onto \(0\le t\le\prod_i x_i^{a_i}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational weighted geometric-mean graph decomposes recursively along a binary tree into three-dimensional power-cone constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in\mathbb Q_{++}\)
\(\sum_i a_i=1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}\mathcal F=\{(x,t):0\le t\le\prod_i x_i^{a_i}\}\)

children.title: Exponential Graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential-cone representation of the scalar exponential epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the closed exponential cone by
\[K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w):v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\le w\}.\]
For scalar \(x,t\in\mathbb R\), the exponential epigraph is the affine slice
\[\operatorname{epi}(\exp)=\{(x,t):t\ge e^x\}=\{(x,t):(x,1,t)\in K_{\exp}\}.\]
More generally, the perspective inequality \(v\exp(u/v)\le w\) with \(v>0\) is represented directly by \((u,v,w)\in K_{\exp}\); closure supplies the cone's boundary at \(v=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential epigraph is obtained by fixing the middle coordinate of the closed exponential cone to one.
assumptions_latex: \(x,t\in\mathbb R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge e^x\iff(x,1,t)\in K_{\exp}\)

knowledge_statements.title: Logarithm Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithm hypograph represented as a fixed-coordinate slice of the exponential cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w):v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\le w\}\). For scalar \(x,t\in\mathbb R\),
\[x>0,\quad t\le\log x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(t,1,x)\in K_{\exp}.\]
Consequently,
\[\operatorname{hypo}(\log)=\{(x,t):(t,1,x)\in K_{\exp}\}.\]
This fixed-coordinate slice contains no point with \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithm hypograph is the exponential-cone slice obtained by placing the logarithm ordinate in the cone's exponential coordinate, and the slice excludes x equal to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(x,t\in\mathbb R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x>0\text{ and }t\le\log x\iff(t,1,x)\in K_{\exp}\)

children.title: Exponential-Logarithm Inverse Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The structural relation between exponential epigraphs and logarithmic hypographs.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Logarithm Inverse Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-transposition correspondence between exponential epigraphs and logarithm hypographs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in\mathbb R\) and \(v\in\mathbb R\),
\[v\ge e^u\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v>0\text{ and }u\le\log v.\]
Therefore the coordinate transposition \(T(u,v)=(v,u)\) maps the exponential epigraph bijectively onto the logarithm hypograph:
\[T\bigl(\operatorname{epi}(\exp)\bigr)=\operatorname{hypo}(\log).\]
Under exponential-cone canonicalization, both statements use the identical membership condition \((u,1,v)\in K_{\exp}\); only the interpretation of the two free coordinates changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Swapping coordinates maps the exponential epigraph exactly onto the logarithm hypograph, reflecting that exponential and logarithm are inverses.
assumptions_latex: \(u,v\in\mathbb R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\ge e^u\iff v>0\text{ and }u\le\log v\)

children.title: Logarithmic Domain Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Positive-domain and closure issues in logarithmic graph representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Logarithmic Domain Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional boundary behavior of the logarithm and its hypograph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The real logarithm has domain \((0,\infty)\) and satisfies
\[\lim_{x\downarrow0}\log x=-\infty.\]
Hence no finite value assigned at \(x=0\) produces a concave extension of \(\log\) to \([0,\infty)\). Its hypograph
\[H=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ t\le\log x\}\]
is closed. Canonical graph formulations must enforce the positive domain implicitly or explicitly and must not replace it by \(x\ge0\) with a finite boundary value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logarithm tends to negative infinity at zero; its hypograph is closed, but no finite concave boundary value at zero exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{x\downarrow0}\log x=-\infty\), and \(\operatorname{hypo}(\log)\) is closed in \(\mathbb R^2\)
