needs canonicalization-system source specifying metadata conflict semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract boundary for conflicting metadata in a compositional canonicalization system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an expression node \(v\), let \(M(v)\) be the set of metadata assignments consistent with all locally inferred properties, and let \(A(v)\) be the set admitted by the composition rule at the parent of \(v\). A metadata conflict occurs exactly when \(M(v)\neq\varnothing\) and \(M(v)\cap A(v)=\varnothing\). If \(M(v)=\varnothing\), the inconsistency is intrinsic to \(v\), rather than a parent-child admissibility conflict. Thus the conflict boundary separates locally coherent expressions from expressions whose metadata cannot be composed in the surrounding syntax.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metadata conflict arises when a node has locally consistent annotations, but none satisfies the admissibility rule imposed by its parent expression.
knowledge_statements.title: Metadata Conflict Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but the definitions of inferred metadata assignments and parent admissibility are canonicalizer-specific and have no cited source.

children.title: Block Separability Recognition System
children.top_down_role: Recognition of additive independence, repeated structure, and matrix blocks.

children.title: Additive Separability Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of expression components that can be organized into independent additive groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Additive Separability Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact additive separability relative to a fixed Cartesian variable-block partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\) and let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). The expression \(f\) is additively separable over this partition if and only if there exist functions \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and a constant \(c\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[f(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=c+\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_i(x_i)\] for every \((x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in X\). A canonicalizer recognizes this property when its supported exact transformations produce or certify such a decomposition; an unreduced multi-block subexpression alone does not disprove semantic separability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expression is additively separable over a fixed Cartesian partition when it equals a constant plus a sum of functions, each depending on one block only.
assumptions_latex: The variable space has a fixed Cartesian partition \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\).
The equality is interpreted as equality of extended-real-valued functions on all of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expression is additively separable exactly when it admits a constant-plus-block-local-sum representation on the full product space.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of additive separability over a Cartesian partition
source needed for graph-canonicalization recognition formulation

children.title: Block-Structure Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of matrix, cone, or variable blocks preserved during canonicalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Structure Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural dependency-set recognition for a finite directed acyclic expression graph and a fixed variable partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each variable leaf \(v\) belonging to block \(i\), set \(D(v)=\{i\}\), and for each constant leaf set \(D(v)=\varnothing\). Process internal nodes only after all their children and assign \[D(v)=\bigcup_{u\in\operatorname{ch}(v)}D(u).\] A node is structurally block-local when \(|D(v)|\leq 1\) and structurally cross-block when \(|D(v)|>1\). Output every block-local node having no parent or having only structurally cross-block parents as a maximal block-local root, together with all structurally cross-block nodes. These sets describe structural block occurrence; establishing semantic dependence or coupling requires additional simplification or dependence analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagate structural block-occurrence sets from leaves to roots; maximal single-block regions form structural block components, while multi-block nodes are coupling candidates.
assumptions_latex: The expression graph is a finite directed acyclic graph.
Decision-variable leaves belong to a fixed disjoint block partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The propagated sets identify maximal structurally block-local regions and nodes containing occurrences from multiple blocks, without asserting semantic dependence.

notation.meaning: set of variable blocks occurring structurally below node v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: dependency-set union is a structural syntax-graph analysis

children.title: Repeated-Structure Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of replicated expression patterns suitable for shared structural treatment.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Structure Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact repeated rooted-DAG recognition modulo alpha-renaming and declared commutative symmetries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each root \(v\), let \(G_v\) be the finite rooted sub-DAG reachable from \(v\), including operator labels, shapes, immutable parameters, edge positions, and shared-node identities. Let \(\sigma(v)\) be a canonical encoding of \(G_v\) that replaces bound-variable names by canonical local indices and identifies child permutations only at operators declared commutative. Distinct roots \(u\neq v\) exhibit repeated structure if and only if \(\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)\). Equality therefore preserves labeled adjacency and sharing while allowing only the declared renamings and symmetries; equality of evaluated values is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two rooted expression regions are repeated structure when their labeled rooted DAGs have the same canonical encoding, including shared-node structure, modulo permitted renaming and commutative reordering.
assumptions_latex: Expression subgraphs are finite rooted directed acyclic graphs with operator, shape, edge-position, and immutable-parameter labels.
Bound-variable names are compared modulo consistent alpha-renaming, and only declared commutative operators permit child reordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeated structure occurs exactly when two distinct roots have equal canonical rooted-DAG encodings under the permitted equivalences.

notation.meaning: labeled rooted sub-DAG reachable from v
canonical encoding of the rooted sub-DAG at v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical labeled-DAG encodings characterize exact repeated structure
source needed for the intended equivalence and parameter-sharing conventions

children.title: Cross-Block Coupling
children.top_down_role: Dependencies that prevent otherwise apparent separability or block decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Block Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic cross-block coupling on a prescribed Cartesian variable partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\) and let \(h:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). Define \(D(h)\) as the set of indices \(i\) for which there exist \(x,x'\in X\), differing only in block \(i\), with \(h(x)\neq h(x')\). The term \(h\) is cross-block coupled when \(|D(h)|>1\) and there do not exist functions \(h_i:X_i\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) for \(i\in D(h)\) and a constant \(c\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[h(x)=c+\sum_{i\in D(h)}h_i(x_i)\] for every \(x\in X\). Thus a multi-block textual occurrence that is exactly reducible to a block-local sum is not a semantic coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A term is cross-block coupled when it depends essentially on more than one block and cannot be written exactly as a constant plus independent block-local functions.
assumptions_latex: The argument space is the Cartesian product \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\).
Equality and block dependence are interpreted for the extended-real-valued function on all of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-block coupling is essential multi-block dependence that does not admit an additive block-local decomposition.

notation.meaning: set of blocks on which h depends essentially

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nonseparability across a Cartesian partition defines semantic cross-block coupling
source needed for canonicalizer-specific semantic recognition

children.title: Embedded Value-Function Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of supported embedded value-function representations.

children.title: Partial-Optimization Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of supported expressions defined through optimization over hidden variables.

assumptions_latex: The hidden-variable feasible-set mapping is nonempty at each parameter point under consideration.
The infimum is interpreted in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expression is a partial-optimization value function obtained by minimizing jointly represented data over hidden variables.

notation.meaning: visible parameter or outer decision variable

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard extended-real representation of a marginal or partial-minimization function
source needed for graph-canonicalization recognition rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal partial optimization with visible parameters and locally quantified hidden variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An expression \(v:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty,-\infty\}\) has a partial-optimization representation when there are a hidden-variable space \(Y\), an extended-real function \(F:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty,-\infty\}\), and a feasible-set mapping \(Y(\cdot)\) such that \[v(x)=\inf_{y\in Y(x)}F(x,y).\] Equivalently, constraints defining \(Y(x)\) may be absorbed into \(F\) by an indicator function. Recognition requires that \(y\) be locally bound by this infimum, while every occurrence of \(x\) remains visible to the surrounding expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial-optimization expression is an extended-real value function formed by minimizing a joint expression over locally bound hidden variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Optimization Recognition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role and marginal-function formula are standard, but no citation supports the graph-canonicalization recognition rule or the stated indicator-function handling.

children.title: Value-Atom Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of registered value-function atoms with available graph implementations.

assumptions_latex: The atom declares its argument domain, curvature, monotonicity, and a finite-dimensional graph or epigraph representation.
The declared representation is valid for every admissible parameter value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A call is recognized as a value atom exactly when its arguments satisfy the declaration and its hidden variables can be introduced locally without capture.

notation.meaning: local hidden variable introduced by the atom

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: value-atom admissibility requires a validated local optimization representation and compatible argument metadata
exact supported-atom declaration format needs source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition criterion for registered atoms defined through embedded optimization values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a registered atom declares \(v(z)=\inf_{y\in Y(z)}F(z,y)\), together with its domain and composition metadata. A syntax-graph call \(v(e)\) is recognized as a value atom precisely when \(e\) has the declared shape, its inferred range lies in \(\operatorname{dom}v\), the declared curvature and monotonicity rules validate the surrounding composition, and a fresh local variable \(y\) can instantiate the representation without capturing variables outside the call. The recognized call may then be replaced by its declared graph or epigraph construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A registered value-function call is recognized when argument metadata matches its declaration and its validated hidden-variable representation can be instantiated locally.
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Atom Recognition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits, but the exact declaration, metadata checks, capture rules, and permission to replace a call by a graph or epigraph construction depend on an uncited atom registry and canonicalizer.

children.title: Hidden-Variable Scope
children.top_down_role: Scoping and dependency boundaries for variables internal to value-function representations.

assumptions_latex: An embedded optimization expression has visible variables \(x\), hidden variables \(y\), and immutable parameters.
The expression graph uses lexical binding for optimization variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A well-scoped hidden variable occurs only beneath its unique binding optimization node and cannot be referenced by sibling or enclosing expressions.

notation.meaning: set of free variables of expression E

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: lexical binding and free-variable exclusion define hidden-variable scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexical scope of auxiliary variables introduced by an embedded value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(v(x)=\inf_y F(x,y)\), the binder \(\inf_y\) owns every occurrence of \(y\) in its body \(F\). Scope is valid if each such occurrence is dominated in the expression graph by that binder, no occurrence of \(y\) lies outside its body, and \(y\notin\operatorname{FV}(v)\). Distinct embedded optimizations must introduce fresh hidden-variable identities, even when their printed names coincide. Visible variables \(x\) may occur both inside and outside the body and remain free unless bound by an enclosing construct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hidden variable belongs only to its embedded optimization body, must not escape into surrounding expressions, and must be fresh across separate value-function calls.
knowledge_statements.title: Hidden-Variable Scope

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lexical-scope condition is coherent, but dominance, free-variable treatment, and fresh-identity conventions require a source defining the intended expression-graph binding model.

children.title: Unsupported Value Representations
children.top_down_role: Embedded optimization structures lacking a valid registered canonical graph.

assumptions_latex: The canonicalizer supports only registered finite-dimensional graph, epigraph, or hypograph templates.
Equivalence must hold for every admissible visible-variable value, not only sampled values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An embedded value expression is unsupported when no registered finite-dimensional template with valid metadata and local variable scope represents it exactly.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: representability by the registered template library is the operational support boundary
support boundary depends on a specific canonicalizer and template library
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational failure boundary relative to a fixed library of exact canonicalization templates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(x)=\inf_{y\in Y(x)}F(x,y)\). The representation is supported by a template library \(\mathcal{T}\) only if some \(T\in\mathcal{T}\) gives an exact finite-dimensional graph, epigraph, or hypograph description of \(v\), validates the required domain and curvature metadata, and introduces all hidden variables with local scope. It is unsupported if no such \(T\) exists, including when the infimum requires an unregistered cone, an infinite-dimensional variable, nonlocal hidden-variable sharing, or merely approximate elimination. Unsupported does not imply that \(v\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value representation is unsupported when the template library has no exact, metadata-valid, finitely representable construction with correctly scoped hidden variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Value Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but support is defined relative to a specific template library whose registered cones, exactness rules, and finite-dimensional representation policy are not cited.

children.title: Canonical Problem-Class Recognition
children.top_down_role: Static classification into solver-relevant canonical problem families.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: A Rewriting System for Convex Optimization Problems
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Problem categories and solver matching
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: A Rewriting System for Convex Optimization Problems

children.title: Linear-Program Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of affine objectives and affine equality or inequality systems.

assumptions_latex: All decision variables are finite-dimensional real vectors.
All objective and constraint coefficients are fixed real data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is a linear program because its objective and feasible set are described entirely by affine functions and componentwise affine inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional minimization-form linear programs with affine equalities and inequalities.

source_refs.locator: 2 From Linear Programming to Conic Programming p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-dimensional optimization model is recognized as a linear program when, after collecting constants and introducing only affine substitutions, it has the form \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\quad c^{\mathsf T}x+d\qquad\operatorname{subject\ to}\qquad Ax=b,\quad Gx\leq h,\] where \(A,G,b,h,c,d\) are fixed real data and the inequality is componentwise. Variable bounds are included as rows of \(Gx\leq h\). Recognition fails under this class if any remaining objective or constraint expression is nonaffine, although a later exact reformulation may place the model in another canonical class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is recognized as an LP when its objective is affine and all constraints are affine equalities or componentwise affine inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Program Recognition

source_witnesses.locator: 2 From Linear Programming to Conic Programming p. 43

children.title: Quadratic-Program Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of supported quadratic objectives and compatible constraints.

assumptions_latex: The decision vector is finite-dimensional and all coefficients are fixed real data.
The quadratic objective is required to be convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is a convex quadratic program exactly when it has a positive-semidefinite quadratic objective and affine equality and inequality constraints.
review_flags: locator discusses conic-quadratic representations and should be checked for the precise QP normal form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex quadratic objective with affine equality and componentwise inequality constraints.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.2 Conic quadratic representations p. 132

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-dimensional model is recognized as a convex quadratic program when it can be written as \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\quad \tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\qquad\operatorname{subject\ to}\qquad Ax=b,\quad Gx\leq h,\] with fixed real data and symmetric \(Q\succeq0\). The semidefinite condition makes the objective convex, while the constraints define a polyhedron. Linear programs occur as \(Q=0\). A model with indefinite \(Q\), or with unequilibrated quadratic constraints, is not recognized under this convex-QP normal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex QP has a positive-semidefinite quadratic objective and only affine equality or inequality constraints; LPs are the special case with zero quadratic term.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Program Recognition

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5.2 Conic quadratic representations p. 132

children.title: Conic-Program Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of models reducible to affine membership in supported cones.

assumptions_latex: Each cone is a fixed closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
Every nonconic expression has been reduced by exact affine substitutions or supported graph constructions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is a conic program because the objective is affine and feasibility is expressed by affine membership in a supported product cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine conic form over a supported closed convex product cone.

source_refs.locator: 2 From Linear Programming to Conic Programming p. 43
2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-dimensional model is recognized as a conic program when it can be expressed as \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\quad c^{\mathsf T}x+d\qquad\operatorname{subject\ to}\qquad Ax=b,\quad h-Gx\in K,\] where \(K\) is a supported closed convex cone, or a finite Cartesian product of such cones, and all displayed mappings are affine. Componentwise inequalities correspond to the nonnegative orthant. Recognition requires every nonlinear atom to have already supplied an exact affine-conic graph representation; unsupported cone membership or a nonlinear residual mapping prevents recognition in this form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic program has an affine objective, affine equalities, and an affine slack constrained to a supported closed convex cone or product cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Program Recognition

source_witnesses.locator: 2 From Linear Programming to Conic Programming p. 43
2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

children.title: Matrix Cone Recognition Family
children.top_down_role: Recognition of matrix inequalities and heterogeneous product-cone structure.

children.title: Semidefinite-Program Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of canonical problems containing positive-semidefinite matrix constraints.

assumptions_latex: The canonicalized problem is finite-dimensional and all displayed coefficient data are fixed real matrices and vectors.
Every matrix variable is constrained to the real symmetric space of its declared dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is recognized as a semidefinite program.

notation.meaning: Cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices of order n.
Trace inner product on symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition criterion for finite-dimensional primal semidefinite form.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Semidefinite cone and semidefinite programs p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonical problem is recognized as a semidefinite program when, after introducing a symmetric matrix variable \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) if necessary, it has the form \[\min_X\ \langle C,X\rangle\quad\text{subject to}\quad \langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i\ \ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad X\in\mathbb S_+^n,\] or an equivalent form obtained by replacing equalities with affine scalar constraints and affine linear matrix inequalities. All objective and constraint maps must be affine in the decision variables; no product of decision variables may remain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recognize an SDP exactly when the objective and scalar constraints are affine and every matrix-domain constraint is an affine positive-semidefinite constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite-Program Recognition

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Semidefinite cone and semidefinite programs p. 139

children.title: Mixed-Cone Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of canonical problems containing heterogeneous product-cone structure.

assumptions_latex: The canonicalized constraint domains are closed convex cones of declared finite dimensions.
Each conic constraint has an affine argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is recognized as a mixed-cone program over the product cone \(K\).

notation.meaning: The j-th declared closed convex cone.
Cartesian product of all declared cone blocks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic and domain criterion for product-cone canonical forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonical problem is recognized as mixed-cone when it can be written as \[\min_x\ c^\top x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax+b\in K_1\times\cdots\times K_q,\] where every block map is affine, every \(K_j\) is a declared closed convex cone, and at least two blocks belong to distinct supported cone families. Equality constraints may be represented by a zero-cone block and free variables by their declared free domains. Recognition fails if any block has an unresolved nonlinear argument or an undeclared domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recognize a mixed-cone program when affine constraint blocks use at least two distinct declared cone families within one product cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Cone Recognition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-cone formulation is plausible, but the defining requirement that at least two blocks belong to distinct supported cone families is an uncited project-specific recognition convention. A direct conic-modeling or canonicalization source is required.

children.title: Matrix-Inequality Recognition
children.top_down_role: Identification of matrix-order constraints eligible for semidefinite representation.

assumptions_latex: The matrix expression is real symmetric for every admissible decision vector.
Its coefficient matrices are fixed and dimensionally conformable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint is recognized as an affine linear matrix inequality and hence as a semidefinite-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition of affine positive-semidefinite matrix inequalities.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 What can be expressed via linear matrix inequalities? p. 144

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constraint is recognized as a linear matrix inequality when it has the form \[F(x)=F_0+\sum_{i=1}^p x_iF_i\succeq0,\] with \(F_i\in\mathbb S^n\) fixed and \(x\in\mathbb R^p\). Equivalently, its affine matrix pencil takes values in \(\mathbb S_+^n\). A matrix inequality containing a nonaffine coefficient, a nonsymmetric unresolved expression, or a decision-dependent matrix dimension is not recognized as an LMI without an additional valid reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recognize an LMI when a fixed-dimensional symmetric affine matrix pencil is constrained to be positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Inequality Recognition

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2 What can be expressed via linear matrix inequalities? p. 144

children.title: Cone-Product Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility limits among cone blocks, target standards, and backend capabilities.

assumptions_latex: Each canonical constraint block has a fixed dimension and a declared cone.
The backend represents Cartesian products by an ordered list of cone blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The block list is compatible with the product cone \(K\) exactly under the stated dimension, order, and family checks.

notation.meaning: Ordered product of declared cone blocks.
Affine block mapped into the j-th cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate for ordered product-cone representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Canonical blocks \(g_j(x)\in K_j\), for \(j=1,\ldots,q\), are cone-product compatible with a backend precisely when each affine map \(g_j:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^{n_j}\) has output dimension \(n_j=\dim K_j\), the backend supports the family and parameters of every \(K_j\), and its required block ordering can be obtained by a permutation applied consistently to maps, offsets, and cone metadata. The combined constraint is then \[(g_1(x),\ldots,g_q(x))\in\prod_{j=1}^q K_j.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone blocks are product-compatible when dimensions, cone families, parameters, and ordering all match the backend representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Product Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Dimension and cone-family matching are plausible, but the claimed precise compatibility criterion, including ordered blocks and consistently permuted metadata, depends on an uncited backend representation contract.

children.title: Backend Routing Capability Interface
children.top_down_role: Selection among exact solver-standard representations supported by available backends.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: A Rewriting System for Convex Optimization Problems
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Analysis phase and candidate solver construction
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: A Rewriting System for Convex Optimization Problems

children.title: Native Affine-Quadratic Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing that preserves recognized linear or quadratic structure.

children.title: Native Linear Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing that preserves recognized linear-program structure for compatible backends.

assumptions_latex: The canonical objective and constraints are affine in a finite-dimensional decision vector.
The selected backend exposes a native linear-program interface for the required variable domains and constraint senses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The routing output is the native linear model together with an inverse map for returned primal solutions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Routing canonical affine data to a native LP interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given canonical data for \[\min_x\ c^\top x+d\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\qquad Gx\le h,\] first verify dimension consistency and backend support for all variable domains and constraint senses. Construct \(M_{\mathrm{LP}}\) by passing \(c,d,A,b,G,h\) directly, applying only documented row permutations or sign conventions. Record the corresponding inverse permutation and sign map. Stop with success after backend validation; output \(M_{\mathrm{LP}}\) and the inverse solution map. Otherwise return an ineligibility result without silently conicizing the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate affine structure, pass linear data to the native LP interface, and retain the inverse mapping needed to recover solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Native Linear Routing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits native linear routing, but direct transfer of the displayed data, validation behavior, supported domains, and inverse-map requirements are interface-specific and have no cited specification.

children.title: Native Quadratic Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing that preserves recognized convex quadratic-program structure for compatible backends.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a convex quadratic and every constraint is affine.
The selected backend supports the required quadratic-objective convention and variable domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The routing output is a native convex quadratic model preserving the matrix \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Routing convex quadratic objectives without conic epigraph expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \[\min_x\ \tfrac12x^\top Qx+c^\top x+d\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\qquad Gx\le h,\] verify \(Q=Q^\top\succeq0\), dimensional consistency, and backend acceptance of the declared quadratic convention. Construct \(M_{\mathrm{QP}}\) by transferring \(Q,c,d,A,b,G,h\), rescaling \(Q\) only if the backend omits the factor \(\tfrac12\). Record all permutations and scalings. Stop with success after backend validation and output the native model plus inverse solution map; otherwise return ineligible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate convex quadratic structure, translate only documented conventions, and route the unchanged quadratic matrix to the native QP interface.
knowledge_statements.title: Native Quadratic Routing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The routing algorithm is plausible but backend-specific and uncited. In addition, the plain statement says the quadratic matrix is unchanged, whereas the mathematical statement permits rescaling it to accommodate a missing one-half convention.

children.title: Native-Form Eligibility
children.top_down_role: Structural criteria governing whether native linear or quadratic forms can be retained.

assumptions_latex: A canonical model and a backend capability specification are given.
Capability checks include objective, constraints, domains, dimensions, and numerical data types.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is native-form eligible if and only if every required feature is accepted without an auxiliary reformulation.

notation.meaning: Set of structural features required by the canonical model.
Set of features accepted by the backend's native interface.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact eligibility predicate for native affine or quadratic routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a canonical model \(M\) and backend \(B\), define native-form eligibility by \[\operatorname{Eligible}(M,B)\iff R(M)\subseteq C(B),\] where \(R(M)\) records the objective class, every constraint class and sense, variable domains, dimensions, coefficient type, and required features such as integrality. The inclusion must hold under convention-preserving permutations, sign changes, and fixed rescalings only. If auxiliary variables, epigraphs, cone lifts, nonlinear substitutions, or relaxation of any domain are required, \(M\) is not eligible for that native form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is native-form eligible exactly when the backend accepts every required feature without auxiliary variables, lifts, substitutions, or relaxations.
knowledge_statements.title: Native-Form Eligibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the eligibility container, but representing heterogeneous capabilities, dimensions, coefficient types, and conventions by the set inclusion R(M) subset C(B) is a project-specific formalization requiring a direct source or backend contract.

children.title: Structure-Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Model features that force routing away from an otherwise native linear or quadratic form.

assumptions_latex: A canonical model has identifiable affine, quadratic, cone, sparsity, or integrality structure.
A proposed route transforms the model before submission to a backend.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The route crosses a structure-loss boundary when the preservation predicate \(P(T,M)\) is false.

notation.meaning: Proposed transformation applied to model M.
Predicate that required native structure and recovery data are preserved.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating convention changes from structure-destroying reformulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A routing transformation \(T\) crosses a structure-loss boundary for model \(M\) when it destroys or obscures a feature required by the selected native interface or by exact solution recovery. Formally, \(P(T,M)\) is false if \(T\) replaces an accepted quadratic objective by an avoidable cone lift, merges typed cone blocks into an unsupported opaque block, drops sparsity or integrality metadata, changes feasible points or objective values, or lacks a computable inverse map from solutions of \(T(M)\) to solutions of \(M\). Mere permutations, sign conventions, and fixed rescalings with recorded inverses do not cross the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structure is lost when routing destroys native features, changes the optimization problem, or omits an exact solution-recovery map.
knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Loss Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the preservation predicate and the classification of avoidable lifts, opaque blocks, metadata loss, and recovery maps are uncited project-specific criteria.

children.title: Cone-Capability Matching
children.top_down_role: Matching required cone families with solver-supported domains.

assumptions_latex: The canonical model has an ordered list of required cone blocks.
The backend declares supported cone families, dimensions, parameters, and product restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model matches the backend exactly when an admissible assignment \(\phi\) exists for all required cone blocks.

notation.meaning: Required cone blocks of the canonical model.
Assignment of required blocks to backend domains.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching required cone blocks against declared backend domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonical model is cone-capability matched to a backend when there exists an assignment \(\phi\) from every required block \(K_j\) to a backend domain such that \(\phi(K_j)\) has the same cone family, dimension, and parameters as \(K_j\), and all backend restrictions on multiplicity, ordering, and cone products are satisfied. Equality or free blocks may match only explicitly supported equivalent representations. Matching is total: if any required block is unassigned, only approximately represented, or supported at an incompatible dimension, the model is not cone-capability matched.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone-capability matching requires a total, parameter-consistent assignment from every canonical cone block to a supported backend domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Capability Matching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matching condition agrees with the node role, but total assignment, exact family/parameter identity, product restrictions, and permitted equivalent representations depend on an authoritative solver-capability specification that is not cited.

children.title: Solver-Specific Standard-Form Routing
children.top_down_role: Selection of solver-native objective and constraint interfaces.

assumptions_latex: The canonical model has passed native-form and cone-capability checks.
The backend specification declares its accepted objective, matrix, bound, cone, and indexing conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs a validated backend-native model and exact recovery maps, or reports that this standard form is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic routing into a selected solver's standard-form interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(M\) and \(S_B\), select the most structure-preserving accepted objective and constraint representation. Apply only the documented permutations, coefficient scalings, triangular matrix encodings, bound conventions, and cone order required by \(S_B\). Construct maps \(E:M\to S_B\) and \(D\) for decoding primal and dual results. Validate dimensions, cone metadata, and the identities of feasible sets and objective values under \(E\). If validation succeeds, output \(E(M)\) and \(D\); otherwise mark this interface unavailable and emit the failed capability checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the backend's most structure-preserving accepted form, encode its conventions, validate equivalence, and retain primal-dual recovery maps.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Specific Standard-Form Routing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm belongs in the routing container, but its encoding conventions, structure-preserving priority, feasible-set and objective equivalence checks, and primal-dual decoding guarantees require a solver-specific source.

children.title: Unsupported Model Routing Boundary
children.top_down_role: Handling models without a supported exact canonicalization route.

children.title: Fallback Routing
children.top_down_role: Selection of an alternative exact canonical route when the preferred route is unavailable.

assumptions_latex: The preferred native route has failed a recorded capability or eligibility check.
A finite ordered list of semantics-preserving fallback reformulations is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns the first validated fallback route, or returns failure when no candidate is valid.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered fallback after failure of preferred backend routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given model \(M\), backend specification \(B\), and ordered transformations \((T_1,\ldots,T_r)\), test candidates in order. For each \(i\), require that \(T_i(M)\) is accepted by \(B\), preserves feasibility and objective values, and supplies computable primal and dual recovery maps. Stop at the least index \(i\) satisfying all checks and output \(T_i(M)\), its recovery maps, and the reason earlier routes failed. If no candidate passes, output routing failure and the complete list of failed predicates; no unvalidated approximation is selected implicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Try semantics-preserving fallback forms in priority order and select the first backend-compatible form with validated solution recovery.
knowledge_statements.title: Fallback Routing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits fallback routing, but the priority policy and the requirement that every acceptable reformulation preserve objective values and provide both primal and dual recovery maps are substantial uncited claims.

children.title: Rejection Routing
children.top_down_role: Termination of routing when no supported exact representation is available.

assumptions_latex: All preferred and permitted fallback routes have been evaluated.
Each failed route has at least one explicit failed capability, eligibility, or equivalence predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is routed to rejection with a finite, checkable diagnostic certificate.

notation.meaning: Finite set of permitted routing candidates.
Failed predicate recorded for route r.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate for rejecting a model from all permitted routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rejection-routing certificate for model \(M\) and backend \(B\) is a collection \[\mathcal C=\{(r,f_r,\delta_r):r\in\mathcal R\},\] where \(\mathcal R\) is the finite set of permitted native and fallback routes, \(f_r(M,B)=\mathrm{false}\) is a failed necessary predicate for route \(r\), and \(\delta_r\) identifies the offending objective, constraint, cone block, dimension, domain, or failed recovery check. The certificate is valid when every route in \(\mathcal R\) appears and each failure is reproducible from canonical model data and the backend capability specification. A valid certificate authorizes rejection without asserting mathematical infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reject routing only with a reproducible failed predicate for every permitted route; this certifies unsupported representation, not model infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Rejection Routing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record consistently presents a routing-rejection certificate rather than an infeasibility certificate, but the asserted completeness and authorization criterion over all permitted routes is a project-specific contract with no supporting source.

children.title: Fallback Priority
children.top_down_role: Ordering among compatible alternative representations and backends.

knowledge_statements.title: Fallback Priority
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic priority rule for routing models unsupported by a preferred backend.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a canonical model and let \((B_1,\ldots,B_k)\) be an ordered list of fallback backends. For each \(i\), let \(A_i(M)\) mean that \(B_i\) accepts \(M\), and let \(P_i(M)\) mean that all required semantics and recovery maps are preserved. The fallback rule selects \[i^*=\min\{i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}:A_i(M)\land P_i(M)\}.\] If this set is empty, routing returns unsupported rather than silently weakening the model. Thus changing backend order may change the selected implementation but not the model represented by an accepted route.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the first fallback backend that accepts the model and preserves its semantics and recovery maps; reject when none does.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) has already failed routing to the preferred backend.
\((B_1,\ldots,B_k)\) is a fixed total priority order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(i^*=\min\{i:A_i(M)\land P_i(M)\}\), or the result is unsupported if the set is empty.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the Fallback Priority leaf and is internally coherent, but the priority, preservation, and rejection behavior is a system-specific routing contract. No cited source supports that contract.

children.title: Unsupported-Model Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Structural reporting for models that reach rejection without an exact route.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported-Model Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-checkable explanation of why no admissible backend route exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a canonical model \(M\), a diagnostic certificate is a tuple \(D=(U,R,T)\), where \(U\) identifies unsupported canonical objects, \(R(u)\) records the rejected capability requirement for every \(u\in U\), and \(T(u)\) records its provenance in the source expression graph. The certificate is valid for a backend family \(\mathcal B\) when \[U\ne\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad \forall B\in\mathcal B\;\exists u\in U:\neg\operatorname{supports}(B,R(u)).\] Each reported object must be reachable from a model output or constraint, preventing irrelevant unsupported objects from certifying rejection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid diagnostic identifies relevant unsupported objects, their required capabilities, and source provenance, and witnesses failure for every candidate backend.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a well-formed canonical model.
\(\mathcal B\) is the set of eligible backends.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) verifiably certifies that no \(B\in\mathcal B\) supports every required object of \(M\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the diagnostics leaf, but this is a bespoke diagnostic-certificate specification. An authoritative source is needed to establish the required-object interpretation of U, the capability predicate, provenance requirements, and the claimed rejection semantics.

children.title: Expression-Graph Canonicalization
children.top_down_role: Dependency-aware lowering of expression graphs through registered atom implementations.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Graph Implementations for Nonsmooth Convex Programs
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Recursive graph implementations
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Graph Implementations for Nonsmooth Convex Programs

children.title: Expression-DAG Traversal
children.top_down_role: Dependency-aware traversal and ordering of expression nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Expression-DAG Traversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependency-respecting traversal used to canonicalize every reachable expression node once.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed acyclic expression graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \((u,v)\in E\) meaning that \(v\) depends on \(u\), first restrict \(G\) to nodes reachable backward from objective and constraint roots. Initialize the ready set with reachable nodes of indegree zero. Repeatedly remove a ready node \(u\), canonicalize it using already stored results for its predecessors, store its result, delete its outgoing dependency edges, and add newly predecessor-free nodes. Stop after all reachable nodes are processed. The resulting order \(\pi\) satisfies \((u,v)\in E\Rightarrow\pi(u)<\pi(v)\); failure to process every reachable node reports a cycle or malformed dependency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Topologically traverse reachable expression nodes, canonicalizing each only after its dependencies and reporting any cycle or malformed dependency.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite.
Canonicalizing a node requires only its data and predecessor results.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every reachable node is processed once in an order \(\pi\) satisfying \((u,v)\in E\Rightarrow\pi(u)<\pi(v)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm matches the traversal leaf and states a recognizable topological traversal, but no source with a specific locator is cited for either the graph algorithm or its canonicalization-specific use.

children.title: Atom Graph-Implementation Dispatch
children.top_down_role: Selection of registered graph implementations for supported atoms.

assumptions_latex: Registry identifiers and priorities are fixed during canonicalization.
Each registered acceptance predicate is deterministic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dispatch returns the valid output of the unique implementation having minimum lexicographic key, or an explicit unsupported-atom result.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dispatch rule selecting a registered graph implementation for each supported atom instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an atom instance be \(a=(t,s,p,c)\), containing atom type, shape, parameters, and curvature-sign metadata. A registry contains implementations \(g_j\) with acceptance predicates \(Q_j(a)\), priorities \(q_j\), unique registry identifiers \(j\), and graph maps \(g_j(a)=(z_j,C_j)\). Form the admissible set \(J(a)=\{j:Q_j(a)\}\). If \(J(a)=\varnothing\), return an unsupported-atom diagnostic. Otherwise select \(j^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{j\in J(a)}(q_j,j)\) in lexicographic order, invoke \(g_{j^*}\), and accept its output only if dimensions and declared cone families satisfy the implementation contract. The dispatcher returns \((z_{j^*},C_{j^*})\) together with implementation identity and provenance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Filter registered atom implementations by applicability, choose the one with minimum priority-and-identifier key, validate the result, and retain dispatch provenance.
knowledge_statements.title: Atom Graph-Implementation Dispatch

children.title: Affine-Expression Extraction
children.top_down_role: Separation and reuse of affine subexpressions during lowering.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Expression Extraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine lowering with reusable coefficient and offset data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For variables collected as \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), every extracted affine expression \(e:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is represented by a pair \((A_e,b_e)\) satisfying \[e(x)=A_e x+b_e\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb R^n.\] Constants yield \((0,b)\), variables yield the appropriate coordinate-selection map, and affine sums and scalar or matrix multiplications are lowered by the corresponding linear operations on coefficient pairs. A cache keyed by expression-node identity may reuse \((A_e,b_e)\); reuse is valid only under the same variable ordering, dimensions, and parameter valuation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent each affine subexpression as a coefficient map plus offset, and reuse it only under identical variable and parameter context.
assumptions_latex: \(e\) is affine in the collected decision variables.
All expression dimensions and the variable ordering are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(A_e\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b_e\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(e(x)=A_ex+b_e\) for every \(x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and finite-dimensional affine formula fit the leaf. However, no source is cited for the extraction rules or for the context conditions governing cached reuse.

children.title: Canonical Object Provenance System
children.top_down_role: Tracking the origin and role of introduced canonical objects.

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Provenance
children.top_down_role: Origin, ownership, and recovery role of variables introduced during canonicalization.

assumptions_latex: Every auxiliary variable is created by one recorded rewrite invocation.
Rewrite output positions are deterministic and unique within an invocation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_X\) is total on \(X_+\) and uniquely identifies the creation record of each \(y\in X_+\).

notation.meaning: source node, rewrite invocation, and output position

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Origin map from introduced variables to the rewrite invocation and source expression that created them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_0\) be the source variables and let \(X_+\) be variables introduced by canonical rewrites. Auxiliary-variable provenance is a total map \[P_X:X_+\to V\times K\times I,\] where \(V\) is the source expression-node set, \(K\) is the set of rewrite-invocation identifiers, and \(I\) is the set of output positions. If rewrite invocation \(k\) at node \(v\) creates its \(i\)-th auxiliary variable \(y\), then \(P_X(y)=(v,k,i)\). Distinct auxiliary identities have distinct creation records, although several auxiliaries may share the same source node and rewrite rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every introduced variable records its source expression, creating rewrite invocation, and output position, uniquely identifying its creation event.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Provenance

children.title: Constraint Provenance
children.top_down_role: Origin and modeling role of constraints introduced by graph implementations or reductions.

assumptions_latex: Every generated constraint arises from a recorded rewrite invocation.
Generated constraints possess stable identities.
Rewrite output positions are deterministic within an invocation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall d\in C_+\;\exists o\in C_0\cup V\;\exists k\in K\;\exists i\in I:(d,o,k,i)\in P_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Origin relation connecting generated constraints to source constraints, expressions, and rewrite invocations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_0\) be source constraints, \(V\) the source expression-node set, \(C_+\) the constraints generated during canonicalization, \(K\) the rewrite-invocation identifiers, and \(I\) the generated-output positions. Constraint provenance is a total relation \[P_C\subseteq C_+\times(C_0\cup V)\times K\times I.\] A tuple \((d,o,k,i)\in P_C\) states that generated constraint \(d\) was produced at output position \(i\) of rewrite invocation \(k\) from source origin \(o\). Every \(d\in C_+\) must have at least one origin, and multiple origins are permitted when a rewrite combines expressions or constraints. The output position ensures that repeated structurally equal constraints remain distinguishable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each generated constraint retains at least one source origin, its creating rewrite invocation, and an output position distinguishing equal constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Provenance

children.title: Cross-Reduction Provenance
children.top_down_role: Preservation of canonical-object origin information across composed reductions.

assumptions_latex: \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) form a type-compatible reduction chain.
Each \(P_i\) relates outputs of \(R_i\) to inputs of \(R_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{1:m}=P_m\circ\cdots\circ P_1\), and stagewise totality implies totality of \(P_{1:m}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional transport of provenance through a sequence of model reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider reductions \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\), where \(R_i\) maps object set \(O_{i-1}\) to \(O_i\), and let \(P_i\subseteq O_i\times O_{i-1}\) be its provenance relation. End-to-end provenance is the relational composition \[P_{1:m}=P_m\circ P_{m-1}\circ\cdots\circ P_1.\] Hence \((z,x)\in P_{1:m}\) exactly when objects \(o_1,\ldots,o_{m-1}\) exist with \((o_i,o_{i-1})\in P_i\), where \(o_0=x\) and \(o_m=z\). If every \(P_i\) is total on generated objects, then \(P_{1:m}\) is total on final generated objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compose adjacent provenance relations across reductions; total provenance at every stage yields total end-to-end provenance.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Reduction Provenance

children.title: Provenance Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where aggregation, elimination, or backend lowering obscures introduced-object origins.

assumptions_latex: Provenance is recovered solely by composing recorded stage relations.
For the final object under consideration, every candidate provenance path to \(O_0\) passes through \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(P_i(z)=\varnothing\), no composed provenance certificate connects that final object through \(z\) to \(O_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at which source recovery ceases to be guaranteed by provenance composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_i\subseteq O_i\times O_{i-1}\) be provenance relations in a reduction chain, and write \(P_i(z)=\{x\in O_{i-1}:(z,x)\in P_i\}\). Source recovery for every final object is guaranteed only if each object on every required provenance path has a recorded predecessor at every stage. If, for some \(i\) and \(z\in O_i\), \[P_i(z)=\varnothing,\] then no composed provenance path that passes through \(z\) can reach \(O_0\). A final object lacks a certified origin for this reason only when all of its candidate provenance paths require that missing link. Non-injective provenance does not itself cause loss: it causes ambiguity. Loss occurs at missing links, discarded identities, or unrecorded many-to-one aggregation unless an explicit aggregate-origin relation is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A missing stage link blocks every end-to-end provenance path that requires it; multiple recorded origins cause ambiguity rather than loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Provenance Loss Boundaries

children.title: Shared-Subexpression Handling
children.top_down_role: Preservation, reuse, or duplication of shared expression structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Subexpression Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Memoized canonicalization preserving one lowered object per shared expression node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an expression DAG \(G=(V,E)\), maintain a memo table \(H\) indexed by stable node identity and canonicalization context. When visiting node \(v\), return \(H(v)\) if present; otherwise recursively or topologically obtain results for all predecessors, canonicalize \(v\) once, store the resulting canonical object, auxiliary variables, constraints, and provenance as \(H(v)\), then return it. Two occurrences share a lowering exactly when they have the same node identity and context key. Structurally equal but independently identified nodes need not share. This rule prevents duplicate auxiliaries and constraints without conflating context-dependent expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memoize lowering by node identity and context so genuine shared nodes reuse canonical objects while merely equal expressions remain distinct.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is acyclic and has stable node identities.
The context key contains every attribute affecting canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each identity-context pair is canonicalized at most once, and every repeated occurrence receives the same cached lowering.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The memoization algorithm fits the shared-subexpression leaf and distinguishes identity sharing from structural equality. No source is supplied for the canonicalization context key, cached artifacts, or reuse guarantees.

children.title: Modular Reduction Systems
children.top_down_role: Composable transformations between recognized categories of optimization problems.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: A Rewriting System for Convex Optimization Problems
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Reductions as first-class transformations
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: A Rewriting System for Convex Optimization Problems

children.title: Problem-Category Analysis
children.top_down_role: Classification used to determine applicable reductions and solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Problem-Category Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound feature-based classification for selecting applicable reductions and solver families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a problem \(P\), compute a feature vector \(F(P)\) containing objective sense, curvature status, constraint families, variable domains, cone requirements, integrality, and parameter-dependent attributes. For each category \(c\) with predicate \(Q_c\), declare \(c\) applicable only when \(Q_c(F(P))\) evaluates true; unknown required features produce unknown rather than false. Return the set \[\mathcal C(P)=\{c:Q_c(F(P))=\mathrm{true}\}\] together with witnesses for satisfied clauses and unresolved features. A reduction or solver tagged with requirement predicate \(S\) is eligible only if the recorded features entail \(S\); otherwise it is rejected or deferred.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extract model features, evaluate category predicates with an explicit unknown state, and admit only reductions whose requirements are entailed.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) has a finite inspectable expression and constraint graph.
Category and backend requirements are represented as predicates on the same feature vocabulary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every returned category has a satisfied predicate, and every eligible route has requirements entailed by \(F(P)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the classification leaf, but the feature vocabulary, three-valued evaluation, witness requirements, and eligibility rule form a system-specific interface with no authoritative citation.

children.title: Reduction Contract Interface
children.top_down_role: Interfaces governing the problem categories consumed and produced by reductions.

children.title: Reduction Acceptance Contracts
children.top_down_role: Problem categories and structural metadata a reduction is permitted to consume.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction Acceptance Contracts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precondition determining whether a reduction may soundly accept a problem instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reduction \(R\) has an acceptance contract \(A_R:\mathcal P\to\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false},\mathrm{unknown}\}\), defined as the conjunction of its required structural, curvature, dimensional, domain, and capability predicates. It may accept problem \(P\in\mathcal P\) exactly when \[A_R(P)=\mathrm{true}.\] Acceptance requires every conjunct to be established from validated model metadata; a false conjunct rejects \(P\), while an unknown conjunct defers acceptance or requests further analysis. The contract is sound when acceptance implies that \(R(P)\) is defined and preserves the declared feasibility, objective, and inverse-recovery semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduction accepts only when all validated preconditions hold; false rejects, unknown defers, and true guarantees the declared reduction semantics.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is well formed in the reduction system's input universe \(\mathcal P\).
Model metadata used by the predicates has been validated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_R(P)=\mathrm{true}\Rightarrow R(P)\) is defined and satisfies its declared semantic-preservation obligations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind correctly matches an acceptance-contract leaf, and the statement is internally consistent. Its three-valued contract and semantic-preservation obligations are architecture-specific and require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Reduction Output Contracts
children.top_down_role: Problem categories, metadata, and recovery information a reduction is expected to produce.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction Output Contracts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface-level contract for a canonicalization reduction and its recoverable metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reduction output contract is a tuple \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{out}}=(\mathcal Q,F,D,I)\), where \(\mathcal Q\) is the output problem class, \(F:\mathcal P\to\mathcal Q\) is the forward transformation, \(D(p)\) is inverse data stored for each accepted input \(p\in\mathcal P\), and \(I_{D(p)}\) maps admissible solutions of \(F(p)\) to solutions of \(p\). The contract requires preservation of optimal value and status and requires \(I_{D(p)}(z)\) to recover every declared model-level primal or dual component whenever \(z\) is a solver result in the stated inverse-map domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The output contract specifies the produced problem class, forward map, stored inverse data, and the model-level quantities recoverable from a reduced solution.
assumptions_latex: \(p\in\mathcal P\) satisfies the reduction acceptance contract.
The reduced solver result lies in the declared domain of \(I_{D(p)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(p)\in\mathcal Q\) and \(I_{D(p)}\) provides the declared status-, value-, and solution-preserving recovery.

notation.meaning: inverse data recorded for input p
solution-recovery map parameterized by inverse data

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this software-interface formalization. Preservation of status, value, and every declared primal or dual component is not automatic for an arbitrary reduction, and the plain statement omits these guarantees.

children.title: Contract Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between the output of one reduction and the accepted input of the next.

knowledge_statements.title: Contract Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composable compatibility of adjacent reduction interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let reductions \(R_i\) and \(R_{i+1}\) have accepted classes \(\mathcal P_i,\mathcal P_{i+1}\), forward maps \(F_i,F_{i+1}\), and inverse maps \(I_i,I_{i+1}\). Their contracts are compatible precisely when \(F_i(\mathcal P_i)\subseteq\mathcal P_{i+1}\), every result produced for \(F_{i+1}(F_i(p))\) lies successively in the declared domains of \(I_{i+1}\) and \(I_i\), and the metadata emitted by \(R_i\) contains every field required by \(I_i\). Under these conditions the composite inverse map is \(I_i\circ I_{i+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adjacent reductions are compatible when each output is accepted by the next reduction and their inverse maps and metadata compose without missing domains or fields.
assumptions_latex: \(R_i\) and \(R_{i+1}\) each satisfy their own input and output contracts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{i+1}\circ R_i\) has a well-defined forward route and inverse map \(I_i\circ I_{i+1}\).

notation.meaning: input class accepted by reduction i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but the proposed necessary-and-sufficient compatibility test lacks authoritative support and does not fully specify inverse-map domains or which stage emits the metadata consumed during recovery.

children.title: Contract Violation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural mismatches that invalidate a reduction or break a composed reduction chain.

knowledge_statements.title: Contract Violation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First interface boundary at which a proposed reduction chain ceases to be valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proposed chain \(R_k\circ\cdots\circ R_1\), a contract-violation boundary is the least index \(j\) for which an accepted input \(p\) yields either \(F_{j-1}\circ\cdots\circ F_1(p)\notin\mathcal P_j\), unavailable metadata required by \(I_j\), or a downstream result outside the domain of \(I_j\). At this boundary the forward chain is undefined or its declared model-level recovery guarantee fails; consequently no validity claim for the complete reduction chain follows merely from validity of its other stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The violation boundary is the first reduction that rejects the preceding output or cannot apply its promised inverse recovery because domains or metadata do not match.
assumptions_latex: Each stage before index \(j\) satisfies its individual contract.
At least one acceptance, metadata, or inverse-domain violation occurs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composite route cannot claim its declared end-to-end transformation and recovery guarantees beyond stage \(j\).

notation.meaning: reduction at the first failing interface
accepted input class of reduction j
forward and inverse maps at stage j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the indexing relies on an unstated empty-composition convention at the first stage, and the metadata failure condition is not clearly assigned to the producing reduction. A source is needed for this taxonomy.

children.title: Reduction-Chain Construction
children.top_down_role: Composition of compatible transformations into a compiler route.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-Chain Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a compatible compiler route from modular reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a problem \(p_0\), a target class \(\mathcal T\), and reductions \(R_i=(F_i,I_i)\) with acceptance predicates \(A_i\). Initialize \(j=0\) and an empty inverse stack. While \(p_j\notin\mathcal T\), choose a reduction satisfying \(A_i(p_j)=\mathrm{true}\) whose output contract is compatible with a remaining route to \(\mathcal T\); compute \((p_{j+1},D_{j+1})=F_i(p_j)\), push \((I_i,D_{j+1})\), and increment \(j\). Stop successfully at \(p_j\in\mathcal T\); otherwise report that no admissible route exists. Recover a solution by applying the stacked inverse maps in reverse forward order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly select an accepting, contract-compatible reduction until reaching the target class, while stacking inverse data for reverse-order solution recovery.
assumptions_latex: The candidate reduction set and target membership test are specified.
Every selected reduction terminates and satisfies its declared contract.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is either a compatible route to \(\mathcal T\) with composite inverse map, or an explicit no-route result.

notation.meaning: inverse data recorded at stage j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the construction leaf, but arbitrary compatible-step selection cannot justify reporting that no admissible route exists. Exhaustive search, backtracking, or a completeness assumption must be specified and sourced.

children.title: Inverse Reduction Maps
children.top_down_role: Reverse mappings used for model-level solution retrieval.

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Reduction Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-level recovery map associated with a semantics-preserving reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a reduction \(F:\mathcal P\to\mathcal Q\) and recorded data \(D(p)\), an inverse reduction map is a possibly partial map \(I_{D(p)}:\mathcal S(F(p))\to\mathcal S(p)\), where \(\mathcal S(q)\) denotes the declared solution record for problem \(q\). For every reduced solution in its domain, \(I_{D(p)}\) must preserve the reported status and objective value and recover the primal variables, dual variables, or certificates named by the output contract. For a chain of reductions, inverse maps are applied in the reverse order of the forward transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inverse reduction map uses stored metadata to translate a reduced solution back into the original problem’s declared variables, duals, status, value, or certificates.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) satisfies its semantics-preservation contract.
The reduced result belongs to the declared inverse-map domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{D(p)}(z)\in\mathcal S(p)\) has the recovery properties declared by the reduction contract.

notation.meaning: declared solution-record space for problem q
metadata retained during the forward reduction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the definition. Status and objective-value preservation and recovery of duals or certificates depend on the particular reduction contract and cannot be imposed universally without a precisely sourced framework.

children.title: DCP-to-Cone Canonicalization
children.top_down_role: Graph-based lowering from accepted disciplined convex models to affine cone programs.

children.title: Atom Graph Expansion
children.top_down_role: Expansion of nonlinear atoms into supported graph representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Atom Graph Expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph or graph replacement of a convex atom by affine conic constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a closed proper convex atom \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) admit the conic epigraph representation \(f(x)\le t\iff \exists u:\ A x+B u+c t+d\in K\), with a closed convex cone \(K\). In any minimization-form DCP expression where the occurrence of \(f(x)\) is monotone nondecreasing, introduce \(t,u\), replace that occurrence by \(t\), and impose the displayed cone membership. Projection onto the original variables preserves feasibility, and minimizing over the lifted variables recovers the original objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace a supported convex atom by an epigraph variable and its affine conic graph constraints; projection and minimization preserve the original model.
assumptions_latex: The atom occurrence satisfies the applicable DCP composition rule.
The displayed conic representation is exact and attained whenever the original atom is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted formulation is equivalent to the original atom occurrence after projection and partial minimization.

notation.meaning: epigraph variable replacing the atom value
closed convex cone supporting the atom representation

children.title: Affine Cone-Membership Lowering
children.top_down_role: Formation of affine expressions associated with product-cone membership.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Cone-Membership Lowering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assembly of lifted graph constraints into one affine product-cone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose canonicalized constraints have the form \(A_i z+b_i\in K_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), each \(A_i\) is linear, and each \(K_i\) is a closed convex cone. Define \(A z+b=(A_1z+b_1,\ldots,A_mz+b_m)\) and \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\). Then the constraint family is lowered to the single product-cone membership \(A z+b\in K\). The original feasible set is exactly the projection of this affine conic feasible set onto the original model variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stack all affine conic constraints into one affine map whose value belongs to the Cartesian product of their cones.
assumptions_latex: Every expanded constraint is an affine membership in a specified closed convex cone.
All introduced auxiliary variables are included in \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A z+b\in K\iff A_i z+b_i\in K_i\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\).

notation.meaning: cone for the i-th canonical constraint
Cartesian product of all constraint cones

children.title: Cone-Family Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Replacement of unsupported composite cones by supported primitive cone families.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Family Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decomposition of product-cone membership into primitive supported cone blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\) and partition an affine expression as \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) with \(y_i\) conformal to \(K_i\). Product-cone membership decomposes exactly as \(y\in K\iff y_i\in K_i\) for all \(i\). If each unsupported block \(K_i\) itself has an exact lifted representation \(y_i\in K_i\iff\exists u_i:\ L_i(y_i,u_i)\in\widehat K_i\), where \(\widehat K_i\) is a product of supported primitive cones, replacing every block by these lifted memberships preserves the projected feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split a product cone into blocks, then replace each unsupported block by an exact lifted representation over supported primitive cones.
assumptions_latex: The partition of \(y\) agrees with the Cartesian factors of \(K\).
Every substituted lifted cone representation is exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decomposed supported-cone system has the same feasible projection as \(y\in K\).

notation.meaning: supported primitive product cone replacing a block

children.title: Conic Inverse-Data Registration
children.top_down_role: Registration of mappings required to recover model-level solutions and duals.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Inverse-Data Registration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Registration of conic rows and lifted variables for primal and dual recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every canonicalized model object with identifier \(r\), record a tuple \(D_r=(J_r,P_r,S_r)\): \(J_r\) selects the conic rows and lifted variables created for \(r\), \(P_r\) maps a conic primal solution to the original primal quantity, and \(S_r\) maps the selected conic dual blocks to the declared original dual quantity with the chosen sign convention. Store these tuples during forward lowering. Given a conic result \((z,y)\), return \(P_r(J_rz)\) and \(S_r(J_ry)\) for each recoverable object; return unavailable for quantities outside the registered domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Record row selectors and primal and dual recovery maps during lowering, then apply them to a conic solver result for each original object.
assumptions_latex: Canonicalization assigns stable identifiers to recoverable model objects.
The conic solver's primal-dual ordering and sign convention are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The registry defines deterministic recovery of every declared model-level quantity from any conic result in its domain.

notation.meaning: selector for conic data associated with object r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but one selector is applied to both primal variables and dual rows despite generally different index spaces. The proposed primal and dual recovery registry is implementation-specific and requires an authoritative source and typed maps.
