children.title: Explicit Affine-Data Extraction
children.top_down_role: Construction of explicit numerical data from symbolic affine canonical expressions.

children.title: Sparse Coefficient-Matrix Extraction
children.top_down_role: Construction of sparse canonical coefficient matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Coefficient-Matrix Extraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Triplet assembly of affine canonical data without dense intermediates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input affine rows \(f_i(z)=b_i+\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}z_j\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Initialize an empty triplet list \(T\) and \(b=(b_i)_{i=1}^m\). For each syntactically present nonzero coefficient \(a_{ij}\), append \((i,j,a_{ij})\) to \(T\); combine duplicate index pairs by addition and discard resulting zeros. Construct \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) in sparse format from \(T\). Output \((A,b)\), which satisfies \((Az+b)_i=f_i(z)\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Traverse affine expressions, collect nonzero row-column-value triplets, combine duplicates, and emit a sparse matrix and constant vector representing every row.
assumptions_latex: Each input row is affine in the indexed scalar coordinates \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\).
Coefficient arithmetic is performed in a fixed exact or numerical scalar model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Az+b=(f_1(z),\ldots,f_m(z))^{\mathsf T}\) for all \(z\in\mathbb R^n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm correctly specifies sparse triplet extraction, duplicate aggregation, and its output invariant, but no algorithmic source or inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Affine Cost-Constant Extraction
children.top_down_role: Assembly of objective coefficients, offsets, and constraint constants.

children.title: Objective-Coefficient Extraction
children.top_down_role: Assembly of variable-dependent objective data.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Coefficient Extraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction of the linear coefficient in an affine canonical objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an affine scalar objective represented as \(f_0(z)=\alpha+\sum_{j=1}^n c_jz_j\), initialize \(c=0\in\mathbb R^n\). Traverse its affine terms and add each coefficient attached to coordinate \(z_j\) into \(c_j\), combining repeated occurrences. Return \(c\). The extracted vector is characterized by \(f_0(z)-f_0(0)=c^{\mathsf T}z\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Collect and combine the coefficients of all indexed decision coordinates to obtain the canonical linear objective vector.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is affine.
The solver-coordinate ordering \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\) is fixed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and characterization of the affine objective coefficient are correct and fit the container, but the record has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Objective-Offset Extraction
children.top_down_role: Isolation and storage of constant objective offsets.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Offset Extraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction and bookkeeping of the constant canonical objective term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an affine objective \(f_0(z)=c^{\mathsf T}z+\alpha\), evaluate its constant component at the zero coordinate and set \(\alpha=f_0(0)\). Pass only \(c\) to a solver whose canonical objective is \(c^{\mathsf T}z\), and retain \(\alpha\) in recovery metadata. If the solver returns value \(v_{\mathrm{can}}\), output \(v_{\mathrm{orig}}=v_{\mathrm{can}}+\alpha\); primal minimizers are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate the affine objective at zero, store that offset outside the solver objective, and add it back to the reported optimal value.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is affine.
The canonical solver omits objective constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha=f_0(0)\) and \(v_{\mathrm{orig}}=v_{\mathrm{can}}+\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Optimal value reported for the offset-free objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The objective-offset bookkeeping is correct for an affine minimization objective and an offset-omitting solver interface, but no supporting citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Constraint-Constant Extraction
children.top_down_role: Assembly of constant terms associated with canonical constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Constant Extraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction of constant vectors from stacked affine constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given affine constraint rows \(f_i(z)=a_i^{\mathsf T}z+b_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), initialize \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) and set \(b_i=f_i(0)\). Extract the coefficient row \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\) into row \(i\) of \(A\). Return \((A,b)\) together with the prescribed row order. Then the stacked affine constraint map is exactly \(F(z)=Az+b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate each affine constraint row at zero to form its constant vector while preserving the canonical row order.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is affine.
A deterministic canonical constraint-row order is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b=F(0)\) and \(F(z)=Az+b\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The extraction algorithm and row-order invariant are mathematically consistent and match the leaf, but the record lacks a cited source and locator.

children.title: Solver Coordinate Index Map System
children.top_down_role: Mappings between model objects and solver-coordinate blocks or rows.

children.title: Variable-Block Index Maps
children.top_down_role: Mappings from model variables to solver-coordinate blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Block Index Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate maps assigning modeled variable blocks to solver-vector positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let modeled variable blocks be \(X_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k}\) for \(k=1,\ldots,q\), after a fixed vectorization. A variable-block index system is a family of injective maps \(\iota_k:\{1,\ldots,d_k\}\to\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with pairwise disjoint images. Packing imposes \(z_{\iota_k(r)}=(X_k)_r\). The recovery map selects the same coordinates, \((\rho_k(z))_r=z_{\iota_k(r)}\). Solver coordinates outside all images are auxiliary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each modeled variable block receives a disjoint injective map into solver coordinates; the same indices pack and recover its entries.
assumptions_latex: Every modeled block has a fixed finite-dimensional vectorization.
The solver variable is \(z\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_k(z)=(z_{\iota_k(1)},\ldots,z_{\iota_k(d_k)})\) and the images of distinct \(\iota_k\) are disjoint.

notation.meaning: Index map for modeled variable block k.
Coordinate-selection recovery map for block k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition gives explicit domains, disjointness, packing, recovery, and auxiliary-coordinate attribution, but no supporting source with an inspectable locator is cited.

children.title: Constraint-Row Index Maps
children.top_down_role: Mappings from model constraints to canonical solver rows.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Row Index Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maps assigning canonical constraint blocks to rows of solver data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let canonical constraint blocks have scalar row counts \(m_1,\ldots,m_p\), and let the solver constraint vector have \(m\) rows. A constraint-row index system is a family of injective maps \(\kappa_i:\{1,\ldots,m_i\}\to\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with pairwise disjoint images. Row \(r\) of block \(i\) is stored at solver row \(\kappa_i(r)\). Pullback of a solver row vector \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) recovers the block vector by \((\eta_i(y))_r=y_{\kappa_i(r)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint injective row maps place each canonical constraint block into solver data and select its corresponding residual or dual entries.
assumptions_latex: Each constraint block has a fixed scalar row order.
The solver row vector lies in \(\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_i(y)=(y_{\kappa_i(1)},\ldots,y_{\kappa_i(m_i)})\), with disjoint images for distinct blocks.

notation.meaning: Solver-row index map for constraint block i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly formalizes disjoint constraint-row maps and row selection, but the record provides no citation or specific locator.

children.title: Reduction-Chain Map Composition
children.top_down_role: Composition of index maps across successive canonical reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-Chain Map Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition rule for coordinate maps across successive canonical reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a reduction chain have forward maps \(P_k:Z_{k-1}\to Z_k\) and recovery maps \(R_k:Z_k\to Z_{k-1}\) for \(k=1,\ldots,L\). The chain maps are \(P=P_L\circ\cdots\circ P_1\) and \(R=R_1\circ\cdots\circ R_L\). If \(R_k(P_k(z))=z\) for every feasible \(z\in Z_{k-1}\), then \(R(P(z))=z\) for every feasible initial point. Index maps compose by ordinary function composition, with later reordering applied after earlier indexing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward maps compose in reduction order, recovery maps in reverse order; stagewise exact recovery implies exact recovery for the entire chain.
assumptions_latex: All consecutive map domains and codomains are compatible.
Each stage satisfies \(R_k\circ P_k=\operatorname{id}\) on its feasible input set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((R_1\circ\cdots\circ R_L)\circ(P_L\circ\cdots\circ P_1)=\operatorname{id}\) on the initial feasible set.

notation.meaning: Forward map at reduction stage k.
Recovery map at reduction stage k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The composition order and stagewise recovery implication are correct and the property kind fits the leaf, but no source with a specific locator supports the record.

children.title: Auxiliary-Coordinate Attribution
children.top_down_role: Bookkeeping for coordinates introduced during graph reformulation.

assumptions_latex: The canonicalized decision vector is \(z\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\).
Original variable blocks and introduced auxiliary blocks have disjoint coordinate assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every auxiliary coordinate has a unique recorded origin and recovery role.

notation.meaning: set of canonical coordinates occupied by auxiliary variables
canonicalization operation that introduced a coordinate
source expression represented by a coordinate

review_flags: Implementation-level formalization lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines provenance metadata for auxiliary coordinates introduced during canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An auxiliary-coordinate attribution for \(z\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\) consists of an index set \(I_{\mathrm{aux}}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and maps \(\alpha:I_{\mathrm{aux}}\to\mathcal{R}\) and \(\sigma:I_{\mathrm{aux}}\to\mathcal{E}\), where \(\mathcal{R}\) is the set of canonicalization operations and \(\mathcal{E}\) is the set of source expressions. For every \(i\in I_{\mathrm{aux}}\), the pair \((\alpha(i),\sigma(i))\) uniquely identifies why \(z_i\) was introduced and which source expression it represents. Coordinates assigned to original variables are excluded from \(I_{\mathrm{aux}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary-coordinate attribution records, for every introduced solver coordinate, the unique canonicalization operation and source expression responsible for it.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Coordinate Attribution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the Auxiliary-Coordinate Attribution leaf, and the notation is internally coherent. However, the uniqueness and provenance requirements are implementation-level design claims with no cited source or inspectable locator. A source defining canonicalization provenance or coordinate-recovery metadata is required.

children.title: Product-Cone Data Assembly Pipeline
children.top_down_role: Population and organization of preselected sparse solver-data structures.

children.title: Symbolic Sparsity-Pattern Construction
children.top_down_role: Structural preparation of reusable sparse data layouts.

assumptions_latex: Each affine coefficient is a finite symbolic expression in parameters.
The canonical row and column index maps are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a reusable sparse layout containing every position that can become structurally nonzero.
review_flags: Implementation-level formalization lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs parameter-independent sparse storage before numerical coefficient evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a symbolic affine matrix \(A(\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), initialize \(S=\varnothing\). Traverse every symbolic contribution assigned to canonical entry \((i,j)\). Insert \((i,j)\) into \(S\) whenever that contribution is not identically zero on the declared parameter domain, and merge duplicate positions. Sort \(S\) according to the chosen sparse-storage convention and construct its pointer and index arrays. The output is this immutable layout together with a map from each symbolic contribution to its storage position; numerical values are not evaluated during this stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Traverse symbolic affine contributions, collect all potentially nonzero matrix positions, merge duplicates, and build reusable sparse index and pointer arrays.
knowledge_statements.title: Symbolic Sparsity-Pattern Construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the structural sparsity-construction leaf. No source supports the proposed procedure, and its exact meaning depends on a specified parameter domain and a sound method for deciding whether a symbolic contribution is identically zero. Those details must be sourced before the claimed reusable structural pattern is reliable.

children.title: Numeric Matrix Stuffing
children.top_down_role: Population of precomputed sparse canonical data structures.

assumptions_latex: A fixed sparse pattern \(S\) and contribution-to-storage map are available.
The parameter value \(\theta\) lies in its declared domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure produces numerical canonical data without changing the precomputed sparse structure.

notation.meaning: stored numerical values of the canonical matrix
symbolic contribution assigned to a storage position

review_flags: Implementation-level formalization lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Populates an established sparse layout at a specified parameter value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given symbolic contributions \(a_k(\theta)\) and their storage map \(p\), initialize every entry of the value array \(v\) to zero. Evaluate each \(a_k(\theta)\) at the supplied parameter value and update \(v_{p(k)}\leftarrow v_{p(k)}+a_k(\theta)\). Populate canonical vectors by the analogous indexed accumulation rule. Contributions mapped to the same position are summed. The algorithm returns the numerical matrix and vectors using the unchanged pointer and index arrays of \(S\); it reports failure if an evaluated contribution requires a position outside \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate symbolic coefficients, accumulate them into their precomputed sparse positions, and return numerical canonical data while preserving the layout.
knowledge_statements.title: Numeric Matrix Stuffing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and indexed-accumulation statement match Numeric Matrix Stuffing. The formula is coherent given the stated storage map, but no source or locator supports the stuffing semantics, duplicate accumulation rule, or out-of-pattern failure condition.

children.title: Product-Cone Block Layout System
children.top_down_role: Bookkeeping for heterogeneous product-cone blocks.

children.title: Cone-Block Dimension Metadata
children.top_down_role: Dimension records for each component of a heterogeneous product cone.

assumptions_latex: The canonical constraint cone is a finite ordered product of supported cone blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metadata determines the ambient dimension and required shape of every cone block.
review_flags: Implementation-level metadata representation lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents scalar and structured dimensions of blocks in a finite product cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a product cone \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_q\), cone-block dimension metadata is the ordered list \((d_1,\ldots,d_q)\). For a vector cone, \(d_k\) is its scalar dimension. For a structured cone, \(d_k\) includes the defining shape parameters and the resulting scalar storage dimension \(s_k\). The metadata is valid only when each shape is admissible for its declared cone type and \(m=\sum_{k=1}^{q}s_k\), where \(m\) is the number of canonical cone rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone-block metadata records each block's type-specific shape and scalar storage dimension, whose sum equals the canonical cone-row count.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Block Dimension Metadata

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate kind for cone-block dimension metadata. The statement is plausible, but structured-cone shape parameters and scalar storage dimensions depend on solver-specific vectorization conventions. No cited source defines those conventions or supports the metadata validity conditions.

children.title: Cone-Block Ordering Conventions
children.top_down_role: Canonical sequencing conventions for product-cone components.

assumptions_latex: The product cone contains finitely many labeled blocks.
A deterministic total order on block labels and types is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convention assigns every block a unique position and makes the serialized product-cone layout deterministic.

notation.meaning: permutation placing blocks in solver order

review_flags: Solver-layout convention lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States determinism and bijectivity requirements for ordering heterogeneous cone blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone-block ordering convention is valid when it defines a permutation \(\pi:\{1,\ldots,q\}\to\{1,\ldots,q\}\) such that \(\kappa(\pi(1))\leq\cdots\leq\kappa(\pi(q))\), with a deterministic tie-breaker yielding distinct positions. The serialized cone is then \(K_{\pi(1)}\times\cdots\times K_{\pi(q)}\). The same \(\pi\) must be applied to block metadata, constraint rows, primal slacks, and dual variables. Thus every source block appears exactly once, and repeated canonicalization of identical input yields identical block order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid convention deterministically permutes cone blocks and applies the same bijection to metadata, rows, slacks, and dual variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Block Ordering Conventions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is a defensible kind for the validity requirements of a block-ordering convention. The deterministic permutation and synchronized transport requirements fit the leaf, but they are unsupported by any citation or inspectable solver-layout specification.

children.title: Product-Cone Offset Maps
children.top_down_role: Offsets linking cone blocks to solver-data row ranges.

assumptions_latex: Ordered block scalar dimensions \(s_1,\ldots,s_q\) are positive integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The offset map partitions all product-cone coordinates into contiguous, pairwise disjoint block intervals.

notation.meaning: zero-based starting offset of block k

review_flags: Implementation-level offset representation lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines contiguous coordinate intervals for an ordered finite product cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For ordered scalar block dimensions \(s_1,\ldots,s_q\), define \(o_1=0\) and \(o_k=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}s_j\) for \(2\leq k\leq q+1\). Block \(k\) occupies the half-open interval \(I_k=\{o_k,\ldots,o_{k+1}-1\}\). Consequently, \(I_j\cap I_k=\varnothing\) for \(j\neq k\), \(\bigcup_{k=1}^{q}I_k=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\), and \(m=o_{q+1}=\sum_{k=1}^{q}s_k\). The inverse offset map sends each coordinate \(r\) to the unique \(k\) satisfying \(o_k\leq r<o_{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prefix sums of ordered block dimensions define disjoint contiguous intervals and a unique coordinate-to-block inverse map.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Cone Offset Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits the offset-map leaf, and the prefix-sum formulas correctly define a zero-based contiguous partition when all block dimensions are positive. Nevertheless, the record has no source or locator establishing the adopted zero-based, half-open product-cone layout convention.

children.title: Heterogeneous Block Validation
children.top_down_role: Consistency checks for mixed cone families and their declared sizes.

assumptions_latex: Each block declares a cone type, shape metadata, and an assigned row interval.
The solver advertises a finite set of supported cone types.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful validation certifies that the heterogeneous block collection defines a consistent solver product-cone layout.

notation.meaning: declared cone type of block k
declared scalar dimension of block k

review_flags: Validation-certificate formulation lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies consistency of mixed cone types, shapes, dimensions, and row intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A heterogeneous block-validation certificate records, for every \(k\), that \(\tau_k\) is solver-supported, its shape parameters are admissible, its induced scalar dimension equals \(s_k\), and \(|I_k|=s_k\). It additionally records that the intervals \(I_k\) are ordered, pairwise disjoint, and cover exactly all canonical cone rows. These checks are directly verifiable from block metadata and offsets. Acceptance certifies that the serialized set \(K_1\times\cdots\times K_q\) is dimensionally consistent; any failed check identifies the offending block and predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The certificate checks supported types, admissible shapes, matching dimensions, and an exact disjoint cover of all canonical cone rows.
knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneous Block Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct role for this validation leaf, and the listed checks would certify dimensional layout consistency. No source defines the supported cone types, admissible shapes, validation predicates, or certificate format, so the exact certificate claim remains unsupported.

children.title: Solver Layout Adapter Family
children.top_down_role: Translation from canonical block organization to solver-native formats.

children.title: Row-Permutation Adapters
children.top_down_role: Translation between canonical row order and solver-native row order.

assumptions_latex: The source and solver row layouts differ only by a permutation.
The permutation matrix \(P\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is orthogonal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adapter preserves the represented affine conic constraint and permits exact recovery by the inverse permutation.
review_flags: Adapter-specific formulation lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents constraint-row reordering with simultaneous cone and dual-coordinate transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A row-permutation adapter maps \((A,b,K)\) to \((\widehat A,\widehat b,\widehat K)=(PA,Pb,PK)\), where \(P\) is a permutation matrix and \(PK=\{Ps:s\in K\}\). Then \(Ax+b\in K\) if and only if \(\widehat A x+\widehat b\in\widehat K\). Solver slack and dual vectors are recovered by \(s=P^{\mathsf T}\widehat s\) and \(y=P^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\). The adapter must permute cone-block metadata consistently with the same row action.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permuting constraint rows, affine offsets, cone coordinates, and dual data together preserves feasibility and allows exact inverse recovery.
knowledge_statements.title: Row-Permutation Adapters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits the row-permutation adapter leaf. The simultaneous transformations of rows, cone coordinates, slacks, and duals are mathematically consistent for a permutation matrix, but no source or locator supports this adapter contract or its metadata requirement.

children.title: Column-Permutation Adapters
children.top_down_role: Translation between canonical variable order and solver-native column order.

assumptions_latex: The source and solver variable layouts differ only by a permutation.
The permutation matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is orthogonal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adapter preserves objective values and feasibility under the bijective coordinate substitution.

notation.meaning: source canonical matrix and objective vector

review_flags: Adapter-specific formulation lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents decision-coordinate reordering and its inverse solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat x=Qx\), where \(Q\) is a permutation matrix. A column-permutation adapter transforms \(A\) and \(c\) to \(\widehat A=AQ^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\widehat c=Qc\), while leaving constraint rows unchanged. Therefore \(Ax+b=\widehat A\widehat x+b\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=\widehat c^{\mathsf T}\widehat x\). A solver solution is recovered as \(x=Q^{\mathsf T}\widehat x\). Bounds, integrality tags, and variable-block metadata, when present, must be transported by the same permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A column permutation reorders decision coordinates and consistently transforms matrices, objectives, bounds, and recovery maps without changing the optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Column-Permutation Adapters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits the column-permutation adapter leaf. The substitutions for the matrix, objective, and recovered decision vector are internally consistent, but the complete adapter contract, especially transport of bounds, integrality tags, and block metadata, lacks cited support.

children.title: Sparse-Format Conversion
children.top_down_role: Conversion among supported sparse matrix storage conventions.

assumptions_latex: The source sparse matrix has finite dimensions and valid indices.
The target sparse format can represent every stored scalar entry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conversion preserves the represented matrix, including the sum of duplicate source entries.
review_flags: Sparse-format algorithm lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts sparse storage while preserving matrix semantics and declared index conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(R_s(A)\), validate dimensions and index bounds, enumerate its stored triples \((i,j,a_{ij})\), translate index bases if required, sort triples by the target format's major index, and combine duplicate coordinates by addition. Construct the target pointer, index, and value arrays, retaining explicit zeros only when required by the declared structural pattern. Return \(R_t(A)\). Correctness requires that for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), multiplication using either representation gives the same vector: \(R_s(A)x=R_t(A)x=Ax\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate and reorder sparse entries, translate index conventions, combine duplicates, and build target arrays representing exactly the same matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Format Conversion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct kind for Sparse-Format Conversion. The intended matrix-preservation criterion is clear, but duplicate-entry summation, explicit-zero retention, index-base translation, and target-format construction are format-specific semantics with no cited source or locator.

children.title: Cone-Layout Adapters
children.top_down_role: Translation of canonical cone layouts to backend-specific interfaces.

assumptions_latex: Source and target layouts represent isomorphic products of supported cone blocks.
Each within-block coordinate transform is an invertible linear map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adapter preserves cone membership and provides inverse recovery of slack and dual coordinates.
review_flags: Cone-layout adapter formulation lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers block permutations and invertible within-block coordinate conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone-layout adapter is an invertible linear map \(T\) satisfying \(T(K)=\widehat K\), formed from a block permutation and admissible invertible within-block coordinate maps. It transforms an affine conic constraint \(Ax+b\in K\) into \(T(Ax+b)\in\widehat K\). Solver slack is recovered by \(s=T^{-1}\widehat s\), while dual coordinates transform contragrediently as \(y=T^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\), so \(y^{\mathsf T}s=\widehat y^{\mathsf T}\widehat s\). Metadata and offsets must describe the target block order and shapes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible blockwise coordinate map transports a product cone, affine rows, slacks, duals, metadata, and offsets between solver layouts.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Layout Adapters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits the cone-layout adapter leaf. The primal and dual coordinate transformations are consistent when the invertible map sends the source cone onto the target cone. However, no source specifies which within-block maps are admissible or supports the claimed metadata, offset, and recovery contract.

children.title: Matrix-Free Operator Lowering
children.top_down_role: Canonicalization that preserves structured linear operators instead of materializing coefficient matrices.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Linear-operator graphs, adjoints, fast transforms, and matrix-free cone programs

children.title: Linear-Operator Graphs
children.top_down_role: Operator-based representations of canonical affine mappings.

assumptions_latex: The canonical affine map is a finite composition of typed linear operators and affine offsets.
All intermediate spaces are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graph represents a well-defined affine map whose evaluation follows any topological ordering.

notation.meaning: linear operator attached to edge e
affine map represented by the graph

review_flags: Operator-graph representation lacks a directly supporting source locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents canonical affine mappings without requiring explicit matrix materialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear-operator graph is a directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\) whose vertices carry vectors in specified spaces and whose edge \(e=(u,v)\) carries a linear map \(L_e\). Source vertices contain input blocks; each non-source vertex computes \(z_v=b_v+\sum_{e=(u,v)}L_e z_u\), with \(b_v\) a fixed or parameter-dependent offset. Designated sink vertices define an affine map \(F:x\mapsto z_{\mathrm{sink}}\). Compatibility requires the codomain of every \(L_e\) to match its destination space. Any topological evaluation order yields the same \(F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A typed acyclic graph composes linear operators and affine offsets into a canonical affine map evaluable without forming one global matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Operator Graphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is appropriate for Linear-Operator Graphs, and the typed acyclic recurrence describes a finite-dimensional affine operator graph. No source supports this particular graph semantics. In addition, the statement mentions multiple designated sink vertices but defines the output using a singular sink; a source-backed version must specify either one sink or an explicit product/stacking map for multiple sinks.

children.title: Adjoint-Operator Generation
children.top_down_role: Compiler support for paired forward and adjoint operators.

assumptions_latex: The operator graph is finite and acyclic.
Each primitive linear map has a registered adjoint rule with respect to the declared inner products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated reverse graph computes \(L^*y\) and satisfies \(\langle Lx,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,L^*y\rangle_X\).

notation.meaning: compiled forward linear operator from X to Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse-mode generation for finite matrix-free linear-operator graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a forward graph for \(L\), traverse its nodes in reverse topological order. Replace every primitive edge \(u=P_i v\) by the reverse accumulation \(\bar v\leftarrow \bar v+P_i^*\bar u\); replace a sum by adjoint contributions to every summand; and reverse a composition \(P_k\circ\cdots\circ P_1\) as \(P_1^*\circ\cdots\circ P_k^*\). Initialize the output cotangent by \(\bar u=y\), initialize all other cotangents to zero, and return the input cotangent \(\bar x\). The result is \(\bar x=L^*y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse the operator graph, apply each primitive adjoint, and accumulate cotangents at shared inputs; the resulting graph computes the adjoint operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint-Operator Generation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the Adjoint-Operator Generation leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no inspectable source supports the compiler graph transformation, accumulation semantics, or registered-adjoint assumptions.

children.title: Fast-Transform Preservation
children.top_down_role: Retention of convolutional, diagonal, Kronecker, and related structured transforms.

assumptions_latex: Every structured primitive provides exact forward and adjoint evaluations.
The target solver accepts matrix-free operator callbacks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lowered representation computes \(Lx\) and \(L^*y\) without forming the full matrix of \(L\).

notation.meaning: cost of evaluating an operator or its adjoint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of exact structured transforms during matrix-free lowering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(L=P_k\circ\cdots\circ P_1\), where each \(P_i\) is represented by a structured kernel, such as a diagonal scaling, convolution, fast transform, permutation, or Kronecker factor. Structure-preserving lowering retains these primitives and their adjoints rather than expanding their matrix entries. Consequently, forward and adjoint applications remain exact and require storage \(O(\sum_i S(P_i))\) and work \(O(\sum_i T(P_i))\), excluding intermediate-vector storage, instead of storage proportional to the number of entries in a materialized matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lowering preserves structured kernels and their adjoints, retaining their application and storage costs instead of constructing a full matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Fast-Transform Preservation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits Fast-Transform Preservation, but the storage quantity S(P_i) is not introduced and the exactness and asymptotic storage/work claims require a source covering the stated lowering model.

children.title: Operator-Materialization Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary between matrix-free lowering and explicit matrix construction.

assumptions_latex: The solver interface either accepts paired operator callbacks or requires explicit coefficient arrays.
All primitive forward and adjoint rules are available before lowering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Materialization occurs exactly at the first interface boundary that cannot consume the matrix-free representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface condition separating callback lowering from explicit matrix construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear subgraph remains matrix-free when every downstream consumer can evaluate it solely through the paired callbacks \((x\mapsto Lx,\ y\mapsto L^*y)\) and any required dimensions or structural metadata. It crosses the materialization boundary when a downstream interface requires indexed coefficients, an explicit sparsity pattern, or a factorization of a stored matrix. At that boundary construct \(A_L\) satisfying \(A_Lx=Lx\) for every \(x\) in the domain; upstream structured nodes need not be materialized separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keep an operator matrix-free while consumers accept forward and adjoint callbacks; materialize it at the first interface requiring explicit coefficients or sparsity.
knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Materialization Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition matches the materialization-boundary leaf, but the assertion that materialization occurs exactly at the first incompatible consumer is an implementation policy requiring inspectable support.

children.title: Parameter-Aware Data Reuse
children.top_down_role: Reuse of canonical structure across repeated solves with changing numerical parameters.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Disciplined parametrized programming and affine parameter-to-data maps

children.title: Parameter-to-Canonical-Data Maps
children.top_down_role: Compiled mappings from model parameters to solver data.

assumptions_latex: The model's expression graph and cone dimensions are fixed over the parameter domain.
Canonicalization introduces no parameter-dependent branching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Canonical solver data are obtained from fixed maps \(D(\theta)=(A(\theta),b(\theta),c(\theta),d(\theta))\).

notation.meaning: canonical matrix, vectors, and objective offset

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-structure parameter maps for a canonical conic problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every admissible parameter value \(\theta\in\Theta\), a compiled data map returns \(D(\theta)=(A(\theta),b(\theta),c(\theta),d(\theta))\) defining the canonical problem \(\min_x c(\theta)^Tx+d(\theta)\) subject to \(A(\theta)x+b(\theta)\in K\). The cone \(K\), dimensions, row and column ordering, and reduction chain are independent of \(\theta\). When the modeling grammar is parameter-affine, each scalar data entry is affine in \(\theta\), so \(D(\theta)=D_0+\sum_{j=1}^p\theta_jD_j\) after compatible vectorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compilation produces fixed maps from model parameters to canonical matrix, vectors, and objective offset while preserving cone dimensions and data ordering.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-to-Canonical-Data Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf, but the asserted affine parameter-to-data formula depends on precise modeling-grammar or disciplined-parametrized-programming hypotheses that are not sourced.

children.title: Canonical-Structure Caching
children.top_down_role: Reuse of symbolic analysis, sparsity patterns, and reduction chains.

assumptions_latex: Parameter values change but expression topology, dimensions, and cone types do not.
Canonicalization decisions do not branch on parameter values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cached symbolic object remains valid for every \(\theta\in\Theta\); only its numeric slots require reevaluation.

notation.meaning: numeric canonical data at parameter value theta

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cache invariant for parameterized canonicalization with fixed graph topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) contain the reduction sequence, variable and constraint index maps, cone block ordering, matrix sparsity pattern, and symbolic parameter dependencies produced by canonicalization. The structure \(S\) is reusable over \(\Theta\) precisely while those objects are invariant under \(\theta\). A cache lookup must therefore be keyed by all structure-determining model features. If any dimension, cone type, graph edge, sparsity position, or reduction choice changes, \(S\) is invalid and canonical structure must be rebuilt.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cache reductions, index maps, cone blocks, and sparsity only while all structure-determining model features remain invariant across parameter values.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical-Structure Caching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits Canonical-Structure Caching, but the claimed necessary-and-sufficient reuse condition and cache-key requirements are implementation-specific and have no citation.

children.title: Incremental Numeric Updates
children.top_down_role: Updating solver data without rebuilding unchanged canonical structure.

assumptions_latex: A valid canonical-structure cache and parameter-to-data map are available.
The new parameter value lies in the cache's admissible structural domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update returns \(D(\theta^{+})\) while leaving every structure field in \(S\) unchanged.

notation.meaning: set of canonical numeric slots depending on changed parameters

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numeric refresh under an unchanged canonical sparsity and reduction structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\theta\), \(D(\theta)\), and a new value \(\theta^{+}\), identify the numeric slots \(I\) whose compiled dependency sets intersect the changed parameter coordinates. Reevaluate only those slots using the stored parameter-to-data maps, overwrite their values in place, and retain all dimensions, index maps, cone blocks, sparsity indices, and reduction metadata in \(S\). If a structural guard fails, stop and request full canonicalization; otherwise output the updated data \(D(\theta^{+})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recompute only canonical numeric entries affected by changed parameters, retaining cached indices and sparsity unless a structural guard fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Numeric Updates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits Incremental Numeric Updates, but selective dependency-based slot reevaluation, in-place overwrite behavior, and structural guards require a compiler-specific source.

children.title: Solver Result Recovery Interface
children.top_down_role: Interpretation of solver outputs through the inverse reduction chain.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: A Rewriting System for Convex Optimization Problems
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Solution retrieval through inverse reductions
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: A Rewriting System for Convex Optimization Problems

children.title: Primal-Variable Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of original variables from solver-coordinate solutions.

assumptions_latex: The reduction chain is finite, and each reduction records a recovery map for every original or intermediate primal coordinate that it eliminates or introduces.
The solver-coordinate result satisfies the canonical constraints to the accepted tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composed recovery map returns the original model variables \(x=R(z_m)\).

notation.meaning: primal coordinates before the first reduction, after each reduction, and in the final solver representation
recovered original model variables selected from z_0
map recovering stage i-1 primal coordinates from stage i coordinates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of recorded recovery maps for primal solver results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let canonicalization produce stage coordinates \(z_0,z_1,\ldots,z_m\), where \(z_0\) contains the original model coordinates and \(z_m\) is the solver-coordinate result. For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(R_i\) recover \(z_{i-1}\) from \(z_i\), including any recorded projection, unscaling, or evaluation of eliminated affine variables. Starting from \(z_m\), compute \(z_{i-1}=R_i(z_i)\) for \(i=m,m-1,\ldots,1\), and return from \(z_0\) the coordinates attached to the original model variables. Thus \(R=R_1\circ\cdots\circ R_m\) and \(x=R(z_m)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the solver-coordinate result, apply the recorded recovery maps in reverse reduction order and then select the coordinates of the original model variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Variable Recovery

children.title: Dual-Variable Attribution
children.top_down_role: Recovery and attribution of dual variables through graph lifts and reductions.

assumptions_latex: Each constraint reduction records its linear residual map and adjoint.
Dual sign and cone-polar conventions are fixed consistently across all reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reverse attribution produces model duals whose pairings with model residuals equal the corresponding canonical dual pairings.

notation.meaning: linear residual map introduced by a reduction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjoint pullback of dual variables through graph reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a reduction whose canonical residual is \(r_c=Hr_m+h\), attribute its canonical dual \(y_c\) to the preceding residual by \(y_m=H^*y_c\), so that \(\langle y_c,Hr_m\rangle=\langle y_m,r_m\rangle\). Traverse reductions in reverse order, summing adjoint contributions when several canonical constraints descend from one model constraint and discarding duals attached solely to auxiliary definitions after their contributions are propagated. Finally apply recorded inverse scalings and sign conversions, and return one dual object for each original constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pull canonical duals backward through adjoint residual maps, summing shared contributions and reversing recorded scaling and sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Variable Attribution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Adjoint pullback is appropriate for this leaf, but dual attribution through lifted constraints depends critically on reduction-specific sign, cone-polar, scaling, and aggregation conventions for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Objective-Value Recovery
children.top_down_role: Reconstruction of model-level objective values after normalization and lifting.

assumptions_latex: Canonicalization preserves feasible objective values through a recorded affine relation with nonzero scale.
The recovered primal point determines every lifted objective variable needed to evaluate the original objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model objective is recovered as \(v_m=(v_c-\beta)/\alpha=f(R(z))\) for an exact feasible solver result.

notation.meaning: recorded nonzero objective scale and objective offset
composed primal recovery map applied to solver coordinates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine objective denormalization after graph lifting and solver-coordinate recovery.

source_refs.locator: 5.3 The Optimal Value Function p. 219
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose canonicalization records \(v_c=\alpha v_m+\beta\), where \(\alpha\ne0\), including any recorded conversion between maximization and minimization. For a solver result \(z\), recover \(x=R(z)\) and set \(v_m=(v_c-\beta)/\alpha\). If \(v_c\) is unavailable or approximate, evaluate the original objective \(f(x)\), provided every required variable is recoverable. For an exact feasible result, \(f(R(z))=(v_c-\beta)/\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Undo the recorded objective scale, optimization sense, and offset; for an exact feasible result, this agrees with evaluating the original objective at the recovered primal point.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Value Recovery

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3 The Optimal Value Function p. 219
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

children.title: Status-Certificate Translation Interface
children.top_down_role: Translation of solver statuses and certificates through the reduction chain.

children.title: Solver-Status Translation
children.top_down_role: Mapping of backend status categories to model-level outcomes.

assumptions_latex: Canonicalization is an equivalence transformation for the status being translated.
Required primal, dual, or ray certificates are recoverable through the recorded reduction chain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A solver status is promoted to the corresponding model status only when its defining certificate survives recovery and validation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate-aware translation from solver statuses to model statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(s_m=\tau(s_c)\) only after checking the mathematical meaning of \(s_c\), the reduction equivalence, and the recovered witness. An optimal status requires a recovered feasible primal-dual pair satisfying the selected residual and gap tolerances; infeasible and unbounded statuses require valid recovered certificates of the corresponding type. Iteration limits, numerical failures, inaccurate certificates, and statuses conflating primal infeasibility with dual infeasibility must remain distinct or be translated to an indeterminate model status rather than to a stronger conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translate a solver status only when reduction equivalence and a recovered witness justify the corresponding model-level claim; otherwise retain an indeterminate status.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Status Translation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate-aware principle fits Solver-Status Translation, but the requirements imposed on optimal, inaccurate, infeasible, unbounded, and indeterminate statuses depend on a specified solver-status taxonomy and recovery interface that are not cited.

children.title: Infeasibility-Certificate Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery and attribution of infeasibility evidence through inverse reductions.

assumptions_latex: The canonical primal system is \(Ax+s=b\) with \(s\in K\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
Recovery maps canonical affine residuals back to the original constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A recovered \(y\) with \(A^Ty=0\), \(y\in K^*\), and \(b^Ty<0\) certifies primal infeasibility.

notation.meaning: closed convex cone of canonical slacks

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic Farkas certificate using the canonical slack convention.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Infeasibility Certificates p. 106
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the canonical feasibility system \(Ax+s=b\), \(s\in K\), a vector \(y\) is a primal-infeasibility certificate when \(A^Ty=0\), \(y\in K^*\), and \(b^Ty<0\). Certificate recovery applies the recorded adjoint reduction maps, inverse scalings, and sign conversions to \(y\). The recovered object is accepted at model level only if its dimensions and cone memberships are valid and its separating inequality remains strict, or satisfies the prescribed numerical margin, when evaluated against the original constraint data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover and validate a dual-cone separator annihilating the primal variable map and pairing negatively with the right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility-Certificate Recovery

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Infeasibility Certificates p. 106
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

children.title: Unboundedness-Certificate Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery and attribution of unboundedness evidence through inverse reductions.

assumptions_latex: The canonical problem is \(\min_x c^Tx+d_0\) subject to \(Ax+s=b\) and \(s\in K\).
The canonical problem has a feasible point, and \(K\) is a convex cone.
The recorded primal recovery maps have well-defined homogeneous parts for recession directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A recovered pair \((d,r)\) satisfying \(Ad+r=0\), \(r\in K\), and \(c^Td<0\) certifies primal unboundedness below.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal recession certificate for a feasible conic minimization problem.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the canonical problem \(\min_x c^Tx+d_0\) subject to \(Ax+s=b\) and \(s\in K\), a pair \((d,r)\) is an unboundedness certificate when \(Ad+r=0\), \(r\in K\), and \(c^Td<0\), provided the canonical problem has a feasible point. Recover \(d\) through the homogeneous parts of the recorded primal recovery maps, omitting affine offsets. Accept the model-level certificate only after validating the recovered direction against the original variable domains, recession constraints, and optimization-sense convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover a canonical recession direction with strictly improving objective slope through the homogeneous primal recovery maps, then validate it against the original model's recession constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness-Certificate Recovery

children.title: Ambiguous-Status Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where backend outcomes do not support a unique model-level interpretation.

assumptions_latex: A canonicalization pipeline maps an original convex problem to a solver problem and provides a status-translation map.
The solver may return statuses that do not include a mathematically checkable certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A status outside the certified cases must be translated to an ambiguous outcome, not to a definitive claim of feasibility, infeasibility, boundedness, or unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for sound translation when a solver status lacks a recoverable mathematical certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\) be a solver-returned status and \(T(s)\) its translation to the original problem. Definitive translation is justified only when the recovery interface verifies the corresponding claim: a feasible point for feasibility, an infeasibility certificate for infeasibility, a recession direction for unboundedness, or an optimality certificate for optimality. If \(s\) denotes numerical failure, iteration limit, inaccurate or indeterminate termination, or if the required recovered object fails its verification tolerances, then \(T(s)\) must remain ambiguous. In particular, failure to produce a feasible point is not an infeasibility certificate, and failure to produce a bounded optimizer is not an unboundedness certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncertified, inaccurate, interrupted, or numerically failed solver outcomes must remain ambiguous; absence of a witness cannot be translated into a definitive opposite status.
knowledge_statements.title: Ambiguous-Status Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and mathematical caution are appropriate, but no source is supplied for the asserted status-to-certificate translation interface or its numerical-status taxonomy.

children.title: Canonicalization Correctness Dimensions

children.title: Domain-Closure Preservation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Preservation of explicit, implicit, open, closed, and limiting domain behavior.

children.title: Explicit-Domain Preservation
children.top_down_role: Preservation of domain restrictions represented directly in the model.

assumptions_latex: Let \(X\) be the original-variable space and let \(I\) and \(J\) be the index sets for the explicitly stated inequality and equality constraints.
Let \(Z\) be an auxiliary-variable space, \(F=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\leq 0\text{ for every }i\in I,\ h_j(x)=0\text{ for every }j\in J\}\), and \(L\subseteq X\times Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Explicit-domain preservation holds exactly when \(\pi_X(L)=F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact preservation of constraints explicitly written in the original formulation.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the original-variable space, let \(I\) and \(J\) index the explicitly stated constraints, and define \(F=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\leq 0\text{ for every }i\in I,\ h_j(x)=0\text{ for every }j\in J\}\). For an auxiliary-variable space \(Z\) and lifted feasible set \(L\subseteq X\times Z\), explicit-domain preservation means \[x\in F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists z\in Z\text{ such that }(x,z)\in L.\] Equivalently, \(\pi_X(L)=F\). This pointwise equality includes boundary points admitted by non-strict inequalities and is stronger than equality of closures or optimal values. Auxiliary variables and redundant lifted constraints are permitted provided they neither remove nor introduce projected original-variable points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonicalization preserves the explicit domain precisely when projecting its lifted feasible set gives exactly the original explicitly constrained feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Domain Preservation

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

children.title: Implicit-Domain Preservation
children.top_down_role: Preservation of domain restrictions induced by atom graph representations.

assumptions_latex: Let \(X\) be the original-variable space, let \(K_0\) index the extended-valued convex expressions, and for every \(k\in K_0\) let \(f_k:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) have effective domain \(D_k=\{x\in X:f_k(x)<+\infty\}\).
Let \(E\subseteq X\) be the explicit constraint set, let \(Z\) be an auxiliary-variable space, and let \(L\subseteq X\times Z\) be the lifted feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Implicit-domain preservation holds exactly when \(\pi_X(L)=E\cap\bigcap_{k\in K_0}D_k\).

notation.meaning: effective domain of the kth expression

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of effective-domain restrictions carried by extended-valued atoms rather than explicit constraints.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_0\) index extended-valued expressions \(f_k:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and define \(D_k=\{x\in X:f_k(x)<+\infty\}\) for every \(k\in K_0\). Given an explicit constraint set \(E\subseteq X\), an auxiliary-variable space \(Z\), and a lifted feasible set \(L\subseteq X\times Z\), implicit-domain preservation means \[\pi_X(L)=E\cap\bigcap_{k\in K_0}D_k.\] Thus every lifted feasible point projects to an original point at which every indexed expression is finite, and every point satisfying the explicit and implicit restrictions has a lifted witness. Replacing any \(D_k\) by \(\operatorname{cl}D_k\) generally defines a different property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lifted graph constraints preserve implicit domains when their projected feasible set equals the explicit constraint set intersected with every indexed atom's effective domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-Domain Preservation

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

children.title: Closure-Behavior Preservation
children.top_down_role: Preservation of open, closed, and limiting graph behavior.

assumptions_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Z\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, with original feasible set \(F\subseteq X\) and lifted feasible set \(L\subseteq X\times Z\).
All closures are taken in the corresponding Euclidean ambient spaces, and \(\pi_X:X\times Z\to X\) is the coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closure behavior is preserved when \(\pi_X(\operatorname{cl}L)=\operatorname{cl}F\) and \(\pi_X(L)\cap(\operatorname{cl}F\setminus F)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closure compatibility, distinguished from exact feasible-set preservation.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51
3.3.3 The boundary structure inequalities p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Z\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(F\subseteq X\), let \(L\subseteq X\times Z\), and let \(\pi_X\) be the coordinate projection. Closure behavior is preserved when \[\pi_X(\operatorname{cl}L)=\operatorname{cl}F\quad\text{and}\quad \pi_X(L)\cap(\operatorname{cl}F\setminus F)=\varnothing.\] The first equality preserves projected limit points, while the second condition prevents an excluded original boundary point from becoming feasible through auxiliary variables. Exact feasible-projection preservation \(\pi_X(L)=F\) alone does not imply the first equality because closure and projection need not commute. Conversely, the first equality alone does not imply exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure behavior is preserved when projected lifted limit points reproduce the original closure and no excluded original boundary point becomes feasible through a lift.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Behavior Preservation

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51
3.3.3 The boundary structure inequalities p. 47

children.title: Boundary-Attainment Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interaction between domain boundaries and attainment after canonicalization.

assumptions_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Z\) be variable spaces, let \(F\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq X\times Z\), and define \(L_x=\{z\in Z:(x,z)\in L\}\) for every \(x\in X\).
Let \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:L\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfy \(g(x,z)=f(x)\) for every \((x,z)\in L\), and let \(p^\star\) be their common infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An original minimizer \(x^\star\in F\) is recoverably attained by the lifted problem exactly when \(L_{x^\star}\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: fiber of lifted feasible points above x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies when boundary optima have actual lifted witnesses rather than closure-only representatives.

source_refs.locator: 5.3.4. Duality and Existence of Optimal Primal Solutions p. 176

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in X\), define \(L_x=\{z\in Z:(x,z)\in L\}\). Suppose \(g(x,z)=f(x)\) for every \((x,z)\in L\), and let \(x^\star\in F\) satisfy \(f(x^\star)=p^\star\). The original minimizer is recoverably attained in the lifted problem exactly when \[L_{x^\star}\neq\varnothing.\] If instead there is a sequence \((x_k,z_k)\in L\) with \(x_k\to x^\star\) and \(g(x_k,z_k)\to p^\star\), but \(L_{x^\star}=\varnothing\), then the lifted formulation represents the value only as a limit and does not attain it above \(x^\star\). Under the stronger condition \(\pi_X(L)=F\), every \(x^\star\in F\) automatically has a nonempty fiber.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An original boundary minimizer is attained after lifting exactly when its lifted fiber contains a feasible witness; an approximating sequence alone preserves only the limiting value.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Attainment Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3.4. Duality and Existence of Optimal Primal Solutions p. 176

children.title: Feasible-Projection Preservation
children.top_down_role: Agreement between original feasibility and projected lifted feasibility.

assumptions_latex: The original feasibility system has feasible set \(F\subseteq X\).
The canonical lifted system has feasible set \(L\subseteq X\times Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is preserved pointwise exactly when \(F=\pi_X(L)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pointwise equivalence between original feasibility and projected lifted feasibility.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq X\) be the feasible set of the original convex problem and \(L\subseteq X\times Z\) the feasible set produced by canonicalization. Feasible-projection preservation is the equality \[F=\pi_X(L)=\{x\in X:\exists z\in Z\text{ with }(x,z)\in L\}.\] Consequently, the original problem is feasible if and only if the lifted problem is feasible. The forward inclusion guarantees existence of auxiliary witnesses for every original feasible point; the reverse inclusion guarantees that no lifted feasible point projects to an infeasible original point. Equality merely after closure is insufficient for this property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Original feasibility agrees exactly with lifted feasibility after projection: every original feasible point has a lift, and every feasible lift projects feasibly.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Projection Preservation

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

children.title: Optimization-Outcome Preservation Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Preservation and recovery of model-level optimization outcomes.

children.title: Optimal-Value Preservation
children.top_down_role: Correspondence of model-level and canonical optimal values.

assumptions_latex: The original problem has value \(p^\star=\inf\{f(x):x\in F\}\).
The lifted problem has value \(q^\star=\inf\{g(x,z):(x,z)\in L\}\), with \(\pi_X(L)=F\) and \(g(x,z)=f(x)\) for every \((x,z)\in L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extended-real optimal values satisfy \(q^\star=p^\star\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real infimum preservation under exact feasible projection and objective agreement.

source_refs.locator: 5.3 The Optimal Value Function p. 219
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(p^\star=\inf\{f(x):x\in F\}\) and \(q^\star=\inf\{g(x,z):(x,z)\in L\}\), with values in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\). If \(\pi_X(L)=F\) and \(g(x,z)=f(x)\) for every \((x,z)\in L\), then \[q^\star=p^\star.\] This equality does not require either infimum to be attained. If the lifted objective depends nontrivially on auxiliary variables, the corresponding pointwise condition is \[f(x)=\inf\{g(x,z):z\in L_x\}\quad\text{for every }x\in F,\] where \(L_x=\{z\in Z:(x,z)\in L\}\); feasible-projection preservation ensures these fibers are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact feasible projection and pointwise objective agreement make the original and lifted extended-real infima equal, whether or not either problem attains its infimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Value Preservation

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3 The Optimal Value Function p. 219
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

children.title: Primal-Solution Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of model variables from canonical solver solutions.

assumptions_latex: A solver returns a lifted point \((\widehat{x},\widehat{z})\in L\).
The canonicalization satisfies \(\pi_X(L)=F\) and \(g(x,z)=f(x)\) for every \((x,z)\in L\).
The recovery interface specifies feasibility and objective tolerances \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{feas}}\geq 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{obj}}\geq 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recovery map returns \(R(\widehat{x},\widehat{z})=\widehat{x}\) only after the prescribed original-problem validation succeeds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection recovery with mandatory validation of feasibility and objective consistency.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a solver point \((\widehat{x},\widehat{z})\in L\), compute \[R(\widehat{x},\widehat{z})=\pi_X(\widehat{x},\widehat{z})=\widehat{x}.\] Evaluate the original constraints at \(\widehat{x}\) and accept the recovered point only when their residuals satisfy the prescribed tolerance \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{feas}}\). When an objective is present, also require \[|f(\widehat{x})-g(\widehat{x},\widehat{z})|\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{obj}}.\] Under exact feasible-projection and objective preservation, an exact lifted optimizer projects to an original optimizer. If validation fails, the algorithm returns recovery failure rather than an original primal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project the lifted point onto the original variables, validate the original constraints and objective consistency, and report recovery failure if validation does not pass.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Solution Recovery

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

children.title: Solution-Set Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between canonical solution sets and model-level solution sets.

assumptions_latex: The original and lifted problems have feasible sets \(F\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq X\times Z\), objectives \(f\) and \(g\), and common optimal value \(p^\star\).
The canonicalization satisfies \(\pi_X(L)=F\) and \(g(x,z)=f(x)\) for every \((x,z)\in L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Their optimizer sets satisfy \(S=\pi_X(\widetilde{S})\) and \(\widetilde{S}=\{(x,z):x\in S,\ z\in L_x\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued correspondence between original optimizers and all auxiliary-variable lifts.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S=\{x\in F:f(x)=p^\star\}\), \(L_x=\{z\in Z:(x,z)\in L\}\), and \(\widetilde{S}=\{(x,z)\in L:g(x,z)=p^\star\}\). If \(\pi_X(L)=F\) and \(g(x,z)=f(x)\) for every \((x,z)\in L\), then \[S=\pi_X(\widetilde{S}),\qquad \widetilde{S}=\{(x,z):x\in S,\ z\in L_x\}.\] Thus every lifted optimizer projects to an original optimizer, and every original optimizer has at least one lifted optimal representative. The correspondence need not be one-to-one unless every optimal fiber \(L_x\) is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting all lifted optimizers gives exactly the original optimizer set, although several auxiliary-variable assignments may represent one original optimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Set Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

children.title: Attainment Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where value preservation does not imply preserved attainment.

assumptions_latex: The original and lifted problems have a common infimum \(p^\star\).
No compactness, closedness, or optimizer-existence hypothesis is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality of infima alone does not preserve attainment; recoverable attainment requires an actual feasible optimizer in the relevant lifted fiber.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates equality of infima from existence and recoverability of minimizers.

source_refs.locator: 5.3.4. Duality and Existence of Optimal Primal Solutions p. 176

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equality of optimal values does not imply attainment. For example, let \(F=(0,1]\), let \(f(x)=x\), and let the lifted problem have \(L=F\times\{0\}\) and \(g(x,0)=x\). Both infima equal \(0\), but neither problem has a minimizer because \(0\notin F\). More generally, if an optimal boundary value is represented only by a sequence in \(L\) whose limit belongs to \(\operatorname{cl}L\setminus L\), then the infimum may be preserved without lifted attainment. Recoverable attainment requires an actual lifted optimizer whose projection is feasible for the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal infima do not guarantee minimizers: an excluded boundary limit may determine the value while providing no feasible point to recover.
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3.4. Duality and Existence of Optimal Primal Solutions p. 176

children.title: Dual-Certificate Semantic Interface
children.top_down_role: Preservation and interpretation of dual information and solver certificates.

children.title: Dual-Variable Semantics
children.top_down_role: Interpretation and attribution of dual variables after reduction.

assumptions_latex: The original conic constraint is \(r(x)\in K\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone and the Lagrangian convention uses multipliers in \(K^*\).
Canonicalization introduces lifted conic constraints and specifies a linear recovery map \(R_d\) for their dual variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A recovered multiplier has original dual meaning only when \(\lambda=R_d(y)\in K^*\) and elimination of auxiliary variables reproduces the original Lagrangian pairing.

notation.meaning: original cone and its dual cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic recovery of original multipliers from dual variables attached to lifted conic constraints.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53
3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the original conic constraint be \(r(x)\in K\), with Lagrangian contribution \(-\langle\lambda,r(x)\rangle\) under the convention \(\lambda\in K^*\). If canonicalization yields a lifted dual vector \(y\), its original dual semantics are specified by a declared recovery map \(R_d\) satisfying \[\lambda=R_d(y)\in K^*.\] After auxiliary variables are eliminated, the recovered multiplier must reproduce the original pairing \(-\langle\lambda,r(x)\rangle\). Components attached solely to auxiliary defining constraints have no independent original multiplier meaning unless the map \(R_d\) assigns them such a role. Sign, scaling, and constraint-order conventions are part of this semantic interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lifted dual variables represent original multipliers only through a declared map that preserves dual-cone membership and the original Lagrangian sign, scaling, ordering, and pairing.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Variable Semantics

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53
3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

children.title: Infeasibility-Certificate Semantics
children.top_down_role: Model-level meaning of recovered infeasibility evidence.

assumptions_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, let \(b\in Y\), and let \(K\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone.
A vector \(y\in Y\) is recovered from the lifted solver certificate using the canonicalization's declared certificate map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditions \(y\in K^*\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\), and \(\langle b,y\rangle>0\) certify infeasibility of \(Ax-b\in K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic infeasibility certificate under the displayed sign convention.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Infeasibility Certificates p. 106
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, let \(b\in Y\), and let \(K\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone. For the conic feasibility system \(Ax-b\in K\), a recovered vector \(y\in Y\) is a directly verifiable infeasibility certificate when \[y\in K^*,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle>0.\] The sign convention is tied to the displayed primal system. Certificate recovery through canonicalization is semantically valid only when the reduction chain maps the solver certificate to this \(y\) while preserving all three displayed conditions. In floating-point computation, certified infeasibility additionally requires explicit tolerances or rigorous residual bounds; an unchecked solver status is not such a certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the displayed sign convention, a dual-cone vector orthogonal to the constraint operator and strictly separating the offset certifies that the original conic system is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility-Certificate Semantics

children.title: Unboundedness-Certificate Semantics
children.top_down_role: Model-level meaning of recovered unboundedness evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness-Certificate Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal unboundedness certificate for a finite-dimensional conic minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the conic minimization problem \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax-b\in K\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a nonempty closed convex cone. If \(Ax_0-b\in K\), \(Ad\in K\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(x_0+td\) is feasible for every \(t\ge 0\), and the problem is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point and a feasible recession direction having negative objective slope certify that the conic minimization problem is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
\(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(Ax_0-b\in K\).
\(d\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(Ad\in K\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_0+td\) is feasible for every \(t\ge 0\), and \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax-b\in K\}=-\infty\).
