children.title: Numerical Consequences of Lift Size
children.top_down_role: Solver-data and conditioning effects associated with unnecessarily large lifts.

assumptions_latex: A primal-dual interior-point method is applied to a conic lift with cone dimension \(N\) and equality count \(p\).
Each Newton step forms and factors a dense \(p\times p\) Schur-complement system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Larger lifts increase memory and arithmetic requirements even when they represent the same projected set.
review_flags: exact complexity depends on cone algebra and sparsity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense Schur-complement model; structured or matrix-free solvers may have different costs.

source_refs.locator: 3 The Geometry of Semidefinite Programming p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated dense linear-algebra model, storing the canonical constraint data requires \(O(pN)\) scalars, while storing and factoring the Schur complement requires \(O(p^2)\) memory and \(O(p^3)\) arithmetic per Newton step. Consequently, \(T\) steps require \(O(Tp^3)\) factorization work, apart from cone-specific scaling operations. Thus an exact lift that unnecessarily increases \(N\) or \(p\) can materially increase storage and solution cost without changing the projected optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a dense interior-point implementation, enlarging a lift increases canonical-data storage and can raise Schur-complement factorization cost to cubic growth in the equality count.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Consequences of Lift Size

source_witnesses.locator: 3 The Geometry of Semidefinite Programming p. 29

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind is appropriate, but the cited geometry chapter does not specifically support the dense interior-point storage and factorization bounds. A source on conic interior-point linear algebra is required, particularly to delimit the cone-specific formation and scaling costs.

children.title: Post-Canonicalization Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Failures arising after a mathematically valid canonical representation has been selected.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Ill-posed problems, scaling, and solution quality

children.title: Poorly Scaled Graph Representations
children.top_down_role: Equivalent graph choices with unfavorable numerical scaling.

assumptions_latex: \(Q=\{z:Az-b\in K\}\) is an exact conic graph representation.
\(D_z\) and \(D_s\) are nonsingular diagonal changes of variable and slack coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalent graph representations can have arbitrarily different coefficient scaling and conditioning.
review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports graph-scaling criterion
conditioning measure is representation- and solver-dependent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling pathology for algebraically equivalent finite-dimensional conic graph forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The scaled coordinates \(z=D_z\widehat z\) and \(s=D_s\widehat s\) yield the equivalent equation \(D_s^{-1}A D_z\widehat z-D_s^{-1}b=\widehat s\), provided the transformed cone is \(D_s^{-1}K\). The representation is poorly scaled relative to the chosen Euclidean coordinates when nonzero row or column norms have a large ratio, or when \(\kappa_2(D_s^{-1}A D_z)\) is large on the relevant linear subspace. Exact projection is preserved by the invertible transformation, whereas residual sensitivity and finite-precision linear solves need not be preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible coordinate scaling preserves the represented problem but can create extreme coefficient ranges or ill-conditioned linear systems, degrading numerical residuals and solves.
knowledge_statements.title: Poorly Scaled Graph Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, and the coordinate transformation is algebraically valid, but no source supports the proposed scaling criterion. The condition number for a possibly rectangular matrix and the relevant subspace must also be specified relative to a solver or linear-system model.

children.title: Cone Interface Mismatch Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Inconsistencies between assembled blocks and solver interface conventions.

children.title: Cone-Block Order Mismatches
children.top_down_role: Disagreement between assembled cone order and backend expectations.

assumptions_latex: The canonical slack is partitioned as \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_r)\in K_1\times\cdots\times K_r\).
A solver interface consumes the same scalar entries using a declared block order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nontrivial block permutation must be applied consistently to data, cone metadata, and recovered dual variables.
review_flags: implementation-interface claim lacks a directly supporting supplied source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch between canonicalizer and solver ordering of heterogeneous cone blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a permutation \(\sigma\), the reordered slack is \(\widetilde s=P_\sigma s\) and belongs to \(\widetilde K=K_{\sigma(1)}\times\cdots\times K_{\sigma(r)}\). A cone-block order mismatch occurs when the numerical rows are permuted by \(P_\sigma\) but the solver is given \(K\), or when the metadata are reordered without applying the same permutation to the rows. Unless every displaced block has an interchangeable cone type and dimension, the solver then tests membership in a different product cone and solves a different conic problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reordering cone blocks is valid only when the constraint rows, cone metadata, and dual recovery use the identical permutation; otherwise the solver receives a different problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Block Order Mismatches

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the mismatch leaf, and the permutation logic is plausible. A solver-interface source is required to support the metadata, row-order, and dual-recovery semantics and to delimit cases in which blocks are interchangeable.

children.title: Cone-Dimension Mismatches
children.top_down_role: Inconsistent cone sizes across metadata, matrix rows, or solver declarations.

assumptions_latex: A canonical conic constraint has slack \(s\in\mathbb{R}^N\).
The declared product cone is \(K_1\times\cdots\times K_r\) with \(K_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface is dimension-consistent exactly when \(N=\sum_{i=1}^r n_i\) and every structured block has its required internal size.
review_flags: implementation-interface claim lacks a directly supporting supplied source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension validation for vectorized product-cone interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_r\) with \(K_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\). The conic interface is dimension-consistent if and only if
\[N=\sum_{i=1}^r n_i\]
and the consecutive coordinate slice assigned to block \(i\) has length \(n_i\). For a structured block, its metadata must induce that same vectorized dimension; for example, a symmetric matrix variable of order \(q\) requires either \(q^2\) full-storage coordinates or \(q(q+1)/2\) packed coordinates according to the declared convention. Failure of either equality is a cone-dimension mismatch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone dimensions are consistent only when declared block sizes sum to the slack length and each structured block uses the interface's stated vectorization convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Dimension Mismatches

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind correctly matches a dimension-consistency leaf, but the structured-block coordinate examples depend on solver-specific full or packed storage conventions. No inspectable interface source is supplied.

children.title: Sparse-Format Mismatches
children.top_down_role: Incompatible sparse storage layouts, indexing conventions, or scalar formats.

assumptions_latex: A sparse matrix is transmitted by index arrays, value array, dimensions, and a declared storage convention.
The receiver interprets indices in its own documented base and orientation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sparse transmission is valid only when the encoded coordinate-value multiset equals the intended matrix after convention conversion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers index base, orientation, dimensions, sorting, duplicates, and triangular-storage conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the intended sparse matrix be \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\). After converting index base, row-versus-column compression, duplicate-entry rules, and any symmetric triangular-storage convention, decode the transmitted arrays as \(\widehat A\). A sparse-format mismatch is present precisely when \(\widehat A\neq A\). Necessary structural checks include equal lengths for index and value payloads, valid pointer endpoints consistent with \(n_{\mathrm{nz}}\), monotone pointers, in-range indices, and declared dimensions \((m,n)\). Passing these structural checks is necessary but not sufficient for semantic equality \(\widehat A=A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse data are compatible only when decoding under the solver's indexing, orientation, duplicate, and symmetry conventions reproduces the intended canonical matrix exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Format Mismatches

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is suitable and the distinction between structural validity and semantic matrix equality is sound. Indexing, duplicate, orientation, and triangular-storage behavior nevertheless require a specific sparse-format or solver-interface source.

children.title: Interface-Level Mismatch Detection
children.top_down_role: Checks that localize malformed solver-data interfaces before result recovery.

assumptions_latex: Canonical data consist of matrix data, vector data, cone-block metadata, and recovery maps.
All declared storage and vectorization conventions are available to the validator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate detects structural interface mismatches before solver invocation but does not certify numerical equivalence beyond the checked invariants.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static certificate for cone metadata and sparse payload consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interface-consistency certificate for \(\mathcal D\) records and verifies: \(N_K=m\); every cone slice is contiguous, disjoint, and ordered as declared; sparse pointers, indices, dimensions, and value counts are valid; structured blocks use the declared vectorization; and primal and dual recovery maps have domains matching the transmitted variable and constraint dimensions. Acceptance certifies that these finite structural equalities and bounds hold. Rejection identifies at least one dimension, order, storage, or recovery-domain mismatch. It does not certify that the canonicalizer's coefficients encode the intended mathematical model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pre-solve validator can certify matching dimensions, block order, sparse structure, vectorization, and recovery-map domains, while leaving coefficient correctness as a separate obligation.
knowledge_statements.title: Interface-Level Mismatch Detection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind is the correct role for this detection leaf. However, the proposed acceptance checks constitute an implementation-level certificate specification with no cited source, and their sufficiency depends on the exact canonical-data and recovery-map interfaces.

children.title: Solution-Recovery Attribution Failures
children.top_down_role: Incorrect recovery of model variables, duals, objective values, or statuses.

children.title: Primal Inverse-Map Failures
children.top_down_role: Incorrect reconstruction of model variables from solver coordinates.

assumptions_latex: A canonicalizer maps each original feasible point \(x\) to at least one lifted feasible representative \(z\).
A recovery routine returns \(R_p(z)\) as the original primal solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal recovery is valid exactly when the inverse map is defined on relevant solver outputs and is constant on representatives of the same original point.
review_flags: recovery-map software semantics lack a directly supporting supplied source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure criterion for reconstructing original primal variables from canonical solver output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(x)\) be the nonempty set of canonical representatives of an original feasible point \(x\). A correct primal inverse map satisfies \(R_p(z)=x\) for every relevant \(x\) and every \(z\in L(x)\). A primal inverse-map failure occurs if \(R_p\) is undefined on a valid returned representative, if some \(z\in L(x)\) satisfies \(R_p(z)\neq x\), or if \(z_1,z_2\in L(x)\) yield \(R_p(z_1)\neq R_p(z_2)\). Thus projection exactness of the canonical problem alone does not certify correctness of the implemented recovery routine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal recovery fails when a valid canonical solution cannot be mapped back, maps to the wrong original point, or depends on the chosen equivalent representative.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Inverse-Map Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no source supports the software-level recovery semantics. Moreover, the conclusion says definedness and constancy are exactly sufficient, whereas correctness also requires the left-inverse condition R_p(z)=x stated in the body.

children.title: Dual Attribution Failures
children.top_down_role: Incorrect association of solver duals with model constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Attribution Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of dual recovery when target constraints do not retain an unambiguous source attribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a source problem be reduced to a conic problem with target dual solution \(y^\star\). For each source constraint \(i\), let \(A_i\) denote the target rows introduced by that constraint and let \(R_i\) be its prescribed dual-recovery map. Dual attribution succeeds only if the reduction metadata determines every \(A_i\) and the recovered multiplier \(\lambda_i=R_i(y^\star_{A_i})\) is invariant under admissible target-coordinate representations. A dual attribution failure occurs when some \(A_i\) or \(R_i\) is missing or ambiguous, or when two admissible attributions produce distinct source multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual attribution fails when canonicalization metadata cannot uniquely associate target dual coordinates with source constraints and recover representation-independent source multipliers.
assumptions_latex: \(y^\star\) is a target-form dual solution or approximate dual solution.
Each recoverable source constraint has a specified target-coordinate attribution and recovery map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists i\) such that \(A_i\) or \(R_i\) is undetermined, or \(R_i(y^\star_{A_i})\) depends on the admissible attribution.

notation.meaning: Target dual-coordinate indices attributed to source constraint i.
Dual recovery map for source constraint i.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

review_flags: canonicalization-specific attribution criterion requires dedicated source

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the leaf, and the statement is internally coherent, but the cited primal-dual geometry section does not establish canonicalization metadata, coordinate-attribution invariance, or the proposed failure criterion. A dedicated reduction and dual-recovery source is required.

children.title: Objective-Recovery Failures
children.top_down_role: Incorrect reconstruction of model-level objective values or offsets.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Recovery Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure to reconstruct the source objective value from a target-form solution and reduction metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the source objective be \(f(x)\), let canonicalization produce target objective \(c^{\mathsf T}z+d\), and let \(x=Pz\) be the prescribed primal recovery. Objective recovery is valid when a recorded map \(Q\) satisfies \(Q(c^{\mathsf T}z+d)=f(Pz)\) for every feasible target point relevant to recovery. An objective-recovery failure occurs if \(Q\), an introduced offset, or a scaling factor is absent or incorrect, or if there exists a feasible \(z\) for which the reported recovered value differs from \(f(Pz)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective recovery fails when missing or incorrect scaling, offsets, or metadata make the reported target value disagree with the recovered source objective.
assumptions_latex: \(z\) is feasible for the generated target problem.
\(P\) is the prescribed source-variable recovery map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(c^{\mathsf T}z+d)\ne f(Pz)\) for some recoverable feasible \(z\), or \(Q\) is not determined.

notation.meaning: Primal recovery map from target to source variables.

review_flags: dedicated canonicalization source needed for objective-recovery metadata and failure criterion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the leaf, but no evidence supports the particular recovery-map model or the claim that equality must hold for every relevant feasible target point. A canonicalization or reduction-recovery source is required.

children.title: Status-Recovery Failures
children.top_down_role: Incorrect propagation of solver outcomes through inverse reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Status-Recovery Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a status translation to preserve the mathematical meaning of a target solver result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_T\) and \(S_S\) be target and source status sets, and let \(\tau:S_T\to S_S\) be the recorded translation. For target data \(D_T\) generated from source data \(D_S\), status recovery is sound only when every returned status \(s_T\) and its certificate imply the semantics assigned to \(\tau(s_T)\) for \(D_S\). Failure occurs if \(\tau\) is undefined or if it maps, without the required recovery certificate, a target status such as infeasibility, unboundedness, or inaccurate termination to a stronger source status whose defining predicate does not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Status recovery fails when translation is undefined or reports a stronger source conclusion than the target status and recovered certificate justify.
assumptions_latex: \(D_T\) is produced from source data \(D_S\) by the stated reduction.
Each definitive status has a mathematical predicate and any required certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau(s_T)\) is undefined or its source-status predicate is not implied by \(s_T\) and the recovered certificate.

source_refs.locator: 5 Self-Dual Embeddings p. 111

review_flags: solver-status translation taxonomy requires dedicated source

source_witnesses.locator: 5 Self-Dual Embeddings p. 111

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the leaf. The cited self-dual-embedding section may discuss certificates and statuses, but it does not directly support this general target-to-source status-translation criterion or its ordering by strength.

children.title: Stale Parameterized Canonical Data
children.top_down_role: Cache invalidation and update failures in repeatedly solved models.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale Parameterized Canonical Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cache invalidation failure for a canonical problem reused after source parameters change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let source data depend on a parameter \(\theta\), and let canonical data be \(D(	heta)=U(G,\theta)\), where \(G\) is the cached reduction graph and \(U\) is the declared update map. After changing \(\theta_0\) to \(\theta_1\), cached canonical data \(\widehat D\) are stale precisely when \(\widehat D\ne D(\theta_1)\). Equivalently, at least one parameter-dependent coefficient, offset, cone dimension, domain restriction, or recovery datum retains its value from \(\theta_0\) although the declared dependency graph requires recomputation or update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical data are stale when a parameter change leaves any dependent coefficient, structure, domain restriction, or recovery datum inconsistent with fresh canonicalization.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) records every declared dependency of canonical data on \(\theta\).
\(U(G,\theta)\) denotes the result required by a correct update or fresh canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat D\ne U(G,\theta_1)\).

notation.meaning: Correct canonical data at the given parameter.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2 Parametric Objective Function p. 96

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.2 Parametric Objective Function p. 96

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind matches the cache-invalidation leaf. The cited parametric-objective section does not support the asserted dependency-graph update model, structural updates, recovery-data updates, or the stated equivalence with stale data.

children.title: Canonicalization Validation Families
children.top_down_role: Validation of symbolic equivalence, generated data, and inverse result mappings.

children.title: Canonical-Form Invariant Checks
children.top_down_role: Structural validation of generated target-form problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical-Form Invariant Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural predicates checked on generated conic-form data before invoking a solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For generated conic data \((A,b,c,K)\) representing \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}z:Az+b\in K\}\), the canonical-form invariant check accepts exactly when dimensions agree, all stored coefficients are finite, and the declared cone product matches the row partition. Writing \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_q\) with block sizes \(m_j\), acceptance requires \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(m=\sum_{j=1}^q m_j\), and every row block assigned to exactly one supported cone \(K_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generated conic data pass invariant checks when dimensions, finite coefficients, cone blocks, and row assignments are mutually consistent and solver-supported.
assumptions_latex: The solver interface uses the membership convention \(Az+b\in K\).
Each declared cone block has a known dimension and supported type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(m=\sum_{j=1}^q m_j\), with a complete disjoint supported row partition.
review_flags: solver-interface and canonicalization validation source needed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits an invariant-check leaf, but the proposed acceptance criterion is solver-interface-specific and unsupported. In particular, supported cone types, finite-data requirements, and exhaustive acceptance conditions require an interface or canonicalization specification.

children.title: Graph Domain-Projection Validation
children.top_down_role: Validation of lifted feasibility, projection, and implicit domains.

children.title: Lifted-Feasibility Checks
children.top_down_role: Validation of feasibility within the lifted canonical representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted-Feasibility Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise validation that a source-feasible point admits the auxiliary variables required by the lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the source feasible set be \(F=\{x:g_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,r\}\), and let the lifted target set be \(L=\{(x,u):A(x,u)+b\in K\}\). A lifted-feasibility check for a tested source point \(x\in F\) passes when it constructs or verifies an auxiliary vector \(u\) satisfying every target cone constraint, within the declared exact or numerical tolerance convention. Exact validation requires \(A(x,u)+b\in K\); a failed witness search is conclusive only when the search procedure is complete or supplies a separation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A source-feasible test point passes when suitable auxiliary variables place its lifted image in every target cone; incomplete witness search alone does not prove failure.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the intended source feasible set.
\(L\) is the feasible set generated by the lifting reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in F\Longrightarrow \exists u\;((x,u)\in L)\) for every tested point, with certified failures distinguished from incomplete searches.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf. The exact feasibility predicate is standard, but the added claims about numerical tolerances, completeness of witness search, and separation certificates need a dedicated validation or lifting source.

children.title: Projection-Equivalence Checks
children.top_down_role: Comparison of projected lifted feasibility with model-level feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Equivalence Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-level validation that eliminating lift variables recovers exactly the source feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the source feasible set, let \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) be the lifted feasible set, and let \(\pi_x(x,u)=x\). Projection equivalence holds precisely when \(F=\pi_x(L)\). A complete check therefore establishes both inclusions: every \(x\in F\) has at least one \(u\) with \((x,u)\in L\), and every \((x,u)\in L\) satisfies \(x\in F\). Finite test samples can detect violations but certify equality only when accompanied by symbolic reasoning or complete set-inclusion certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection equivalence requires both that every source-feasible point has a feasible lift and that every feasible lift projects to a source-feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(L\) use the same source-variable coordinates \(x\).
\(\pi_x\) discards only auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\pi_x(L)=\{x:\exists u,\ (x,u)\in L\}\).
review_flags: dedicated extended-formulation or graph-canonicalization source needed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, and the equality F=pi_x(L) correctly expresses projection equivalence. No source is supplied for the broader validation and certification claims, including when finite sampling can certify equality.

children.title: Explicit-Domain Checks
children.top_down_role: Validation of domain restrictions represented directly in canonical constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Domain Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validation that explicitly generated constraints enforce the declared domain of every source atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each source atom \(h_j\) with declared domain \(D_j\), let \(E_j(x,u)\in K_j\) be the target constraints generated specifically to enforce that domain. The explicit-domain check passes when target feasibility implies that the recovered argument \(a_j(x)\) belongs to \(D_j\), and when every source-feasible argument admits auxiliary values satisfying the generated constraints. Thus the required predicate is \(a_j(x)\in D_j\Longleftrightarrow\exists u_j\;E_j(x,u_j)\in K_j\), subject to the canonicalizer's stated boundary convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit domain constraints are correct when their feasible projection equals the atom's declared domain, including the chosen treatment of boundary points.
assumptions_latex: Each source atom \(h_j\) has a declared domain \(D_j\).
\(E_j(x,u_j)\in K_j\) is the complete generated subsystem for that domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_j(x)\in D_j\Longleftrightarrow\exists u_j\;E_j(x,u_j)\in K_j\) for every atom \(j\).

notation.meaning: Declared domain of source atom j.
Argument supplied to source atom j.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but no source supports the asserted biconditional for each generated domain subsystem or the boundary-convention qualification. These depend on the canonicalizer's atom and domain semantics.

children.title: Implicit-Domain Checks
children.top_down_role: Validation of domain restrictions induced by graph templates.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-Domain Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validation that graph constraints enforce atom domains even without separately emitted domain constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a source atom \(h\) have domain \(D\), and let \(G_h\subseteq X\times T\times U\) be its generated graph or epigraph lift. When no separate constraint \(x\in D\) is emitted, the implicit-domain check passes precisely when feasibility of the graph subsystem enforces the domain and does not exclude valid arguments: \(x\in D\Longleftrightarrow\exists(t,u)\;((x,t,u)\in G_h)\), with the quantification over \(t\) restricted by the source relation being represented. In particular, every feasible generated tuple must satisfy \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit domain is correct when feasibility of the atom's graph lift admits exactly the valid source arguments and rejects every out-of-domain argument.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is the intended domain of atom \(h\).
\(G_h\) is the complete generated subsystem representing the atom relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_x(G_h)=D\) under the represented relation's quantification over \(t\).

notation.meaning: Generated graph or epigraph lift for the atom.

review_flags: exact quantification depends on graph versus epigraph representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but the quantification over t is not stated precisely. Graph and epigraph representations generally impose different relations and cannot be combined through the phrase 'restricted by the source relation.' A dedicated source is needed to select and state the correct variant.

children.title: Closure-Boundary Checks
children.top_down_role: Validation of open, closed, and limiting boundary behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Boundary Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validation that canonicalization preserves open, closed, and limiting behavior at domain boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the source graph or epigraph set and \(L\) its generated lifted set, with recovery projection \(\pi\). A closure-boundary check requires the canonicalizer to declare whether it represents \(S\) or its closure \(\operatorname{cl}S\). It passes when \(\pi(L)=S\) in the exact convention, or \(\pi(L)=\operatorname{cl}S\) in a declared closed-extension convention, and when every boundary point in \(\operatorname{cl}S\setminus S\) is respectively rejected or identified as a closure-only point. Undeclared replacement of \(S\) by \(\operatorname{cl}S\) fails the check.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary validation checks whether the lift represents the original graph or a declared closure and correctly classifies closure-only boundary points.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is the intended source graph or epigraph set.
\(L\) is the generated lift and \(\pi\) is its recovery projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(L)=S\) or \(\pi(L)=\operatorname{cl}S\) according to the declared convention, with \(\operatorname{cl}S\setminus S\) classified explicitly.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.3 The boundary structure inequalities p. 47

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.3 The boundary structure inequalities p. 47

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf. The cited boundary-structure section does not directly support the canonicalizer-specific alternatives pi(L)=S versus pi(L)=cl S or the required classification of closure-only points.

children.title: Reduction-Recovery Round-Trip Checks
children.top_down_role: Validation of forward reductions and inverse result recovery.

children.title: Forward-Reduction Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency of model-to-canonical transformations across the reduction chain.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward-Reduction Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency of repeated forward reduction with the recorded canonicalization map and parameter state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a deterministic canonicalization map from admissible source data \(D_S\) to target data and recovery metadata, \(C(D_S)=(D_T,M)\). Forward-reduction consistency holds when two executions on the same source data and canonicalization options produce equivalent target problems and compatible metadata. Precisely, if \(C_1(D_S)=(D_T^{(1)},M_1)\) and \(C_2(D_S)=(D_T^{(2)},M_2)\), there must exist a declared target-coordinate isomorphism \(T\) carrying \(D_T^{(1)}\) to \(D_T^{(2)}\) and intertwining the associated recovery maps; under canonical ordering, equality is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated reduction of identical source data must yield identical canonical data, or equivalent data under a declared coordinate isomorphism, with compatible recovery metadata.
assumptions_latex: The source data and all canonicalization options are identical across executions.
Any permitted nondeterminism is represented by a declared target-coordinate isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_T^{(2)}=T(D_T^{(1)})\) and the recovery maps encoded by \(M_1,M_2\) commute with \(T\).
review_flags: dedicated canonicalization determinism and equivalence source needed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind is suitable for this consistency leaf, but no source defines the permitted target-coordinate isomorphism, how it acts on target data, or the required intertwining of recovery maps. The criterion therefore remains implementation-specific and under-specified.

children.title: Primal-Recovery Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency of recovered model variables with canonical solver results.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Recovery Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round-trip agreement between source points, their forward lifts, and recovered primal variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) map a source point \(x\) and admissible auxiliary choice \(u\) to a target point \(z=F(x,u)\), and let \(R_p\) be the prescribed primal-recovery map. Primal-recovery consistency requires \(R_p(F(x,u))=x\) for every source-feasible \(x\) and every admissible lift used by the reduction. Conversely, for every target-feasible \(z\), the recovered point \(R_p(z)\) must be source-feasible and must agree with all source-variable coordinates retained in \(z\). Under numerical recovery, both equalities use one explicitly declared tolerance and scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal recovery is consistent when it returns each source point from every admissible lift and maps every target-feasible point back to a source-feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the forward point-lifting map associated with the reduction.
\(R_p\) is the recorded primal-recovery map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_p(F(x,u))=x\) for admissible \((x,u)\), and target feasibility of \(z\) implies source feasibility of \(R_p(z)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the consistency leaf, but no source supports the two-sided round-trip requirements. The numerical variant also lacks a defined norm, residual, scaling rule, and tolerance predicate.

children.title: Dual-Recovery Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency of recovered dual information with its model-level attribution.

assumptions_latex: The original convex problem \(P\) and canonical conic problem \(C\) have Lagrange duals with attained solutions.
Canonicalization provides a dual recovery map \(R_d\) and an adjoint-consistent correspondence between original and canonical constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_d(y_C^\star)\) is dual feasible for \(P\), has the same dual objective value as \(y_C^\star\), and satisfies the original KKT conditions with the recovered primal point.

notation.meaning: Dual-variable recovery map from the canonical problem to the original problem.
An optimal dual solution of the canonical problem.

review_flags: abstract recovery-map formulation should be checked against a canonicalization-specific reference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dual recovery under attained primal-dual optima and an adjoint-consistent canonicalization.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dual-recovery consistency holds when, for every canonical primal-dual optimum \((z_C^\star,y_C^\star)\), the recovered multiplier \(y_P^\star=R_d(y_C^\star)\) is feasible for the dual of \(P\), obeys \(d_P(y_P^\star)=d_C(y_C^\star)\), and, together with the recovered primal point \(x_P^\star\), satisfies primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementary slackness, and stationarity for \(P\). Multipliers introduced solely by graph expansion may be eliminated, but their elimination must preserve the stationarity equation in the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovered canonical multipliers must be feasible and optimal for the original dual and must reproduce every original KKT relation.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Recovery Consistency

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited dual-geometry section does not specifically support transport of multipliers through canonicalization. Adjoint consistency alone does not establish preservation of dual objectives and every original KKT relation, particularly when graph expansion introduces eliminable multipliers or objective offsets.

children.title: Certificate-Recovery Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency of recovered certificates with the originating model.

assumptions_latex: Canonicalization supplies recovery maps for primal points, dual points, and solver certificates.
Certificate predicates are evaluated using exact arithmetic or explicitly stated numerical tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted canonical certificate recovers to a valid certificate of the corresponding original claim.

notation.meaning: Canonicalization map from original problem data to canonical problem data.
Predicates validating original and canonical certificates.

review_flags: needs a source treating certificate transport through canonicalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validation predicate for recovering optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Certificate-recovery consistency requires that, for each supported claim type \(s\) and every canonical certificate \(w_C\), \[V_C(T(P),s,w_C)=\mathrm{true}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad V_P(P,s,R_c(w_C))=\mathrm{true}.\] For an optimality claim, the recovered object must verify primal and dual feasibility and the asserted gap. For infeasibility or unboundedness, it must satisfy the original separating-ray or improving-ray equations, including the required sign and strictness condition. A certificate is rejected whenever recovery discards data needed to evaluate \(V_P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical certificate is consistent only if its recovered object directly verifies the same claim for the original problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate-Recovery Consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication is a plausible validation condition, but no source supports certificate transport for optimality, infeasibility, and unboundedness. The record describes a consistency condition rather than presenting a certificate itself, so content_kind should be condition once sourced.

children.title: Status-Translation Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency of model-level statuses across forward and inverse mappings.

assumptions_latex: The original and canonical formulations use specified status sets and explicit semantic definitions for every status.
Canonicalization is exact on feasible points, recession directions, and relevant closure assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The translated canonical status denotes exactly the corresponding mathematical status of the original problem.

notation.meaning: Semantic predicate asserting that problem Q has status s.

review_flags: solver-specific ambiguous and inaccurate statuses are outside the exact formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact translation of mathematical statuses, excluding implementation-specific unknown or inaccurate outcomes.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.3 Robust solvability status p. 64

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Status-translation consistency holds when, for every supported canonical status \(s_C\in\mathcal S_C\), \[\Phi(C,s_C)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Phi(P,\tau(s_C)).\] Thus canonical optimality translates to original optimality with equal value; canonical infeasibility translates to original infeasibility; and canonical unboundedness translates only when its improving direction recovers to an original improving recession direction. If attainment, closure, or duality assumptions differ between formulations, statuses such as infeasible, dual infeasible, and unbounded may not be interchanged without an additional certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A translated status must express the same feasibility, optimality, or recession fact for the original and canonical problems.
knowledge_statements.title: Status-Translation Consistency

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.3 Robust solvability status p. 64

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited solvability-status section does not establish status equivalence under canonicalization. Exact preservation of infeasibility, unboundedness, attainment, closure, and dual statuses requires a reformulation-specific source and more explicit status semantics.

children.title: Cross-Route Concordance Checks
children.top_down_role: Comparison of alternative exact graph implementations and solver routes.

children.title: Exact-Representation Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Comparison of model outcomes across alternative exact graph representations.

assumptions_latex: Two canonicalization routes are applied to the same original problem and use exact arithmetic.
Each route has a projection from its lifted feasible set to the original decision space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The routes have identical projected feasible sets and objective values on corresponding feasible lifts, hence identical optimal values and original minimizers.

notation.meaning: Feasible sets produced by canonicalization routes one and two.
Projections from lifted variables to original variables.
Objectives in the two canonical representations.

review_flags: abstract projected-epigraph formulation should be matched to the project canonicalization calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence of two lifted canonical representations after projection to original variables.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.3 Tractable representation of (2.17): general case p. 44

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two canonical routes are exactly representation-equivalent when \[\pi_1(F_1)=\pi_2(F_2)\] and, for every \(x\) in this common projection, \[\inf\{f_1(z_1):z_1\in F_1,\ \pi_1(z_1)=x\}=\inf\{f_2(z_2):z_2\in F_2,\ \pi_2(z_2)=x\}.\] Consequently, both routes induce the same extended-valued objective on the original variable space, the same optimal value, and the same set of optimal original decisions. Equality of lifted feasible sets is unnecessary because auxiliary variables may differ between routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two routes are exactly equivalent when projection yields the same feasible original points and the same minimized objective at each point.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Representation Equivalence

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.3 Tractable representation of (2.17): general case p. 44

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited section concerns a particular tractable representation and does not clearly support this general cross-route equivalence criterion. Moreover, conclusion_latex claims equality on corresponding feasible lifts, whereas the statement requires only equality of fiberwise infima; those are not equivalent claims.

children.title: Backend Result Concordance
children.top_down_role: Comparison of primal, dual, and objective results across supported backends.

assumptions_latex: Two backends solve exactly equivalent canonical representations of the same convex problem.
Each reported solution passes its backend's stated feasibility and optimality tolerances, transported to common original-space tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted backend results agree on the recovered objective value and recovered solution set up to the declared tolerances.

notation.meaning: Recovered original-space outputs from backends one and two.

review_flags: needs a source specifying backend-independent numerical concordance criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-aware comparison of recovered results from distinct solver backends.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Backend result concordance holds when both accepted outputs recover to points satisfying the same original constraints within the common feasibility tolerance and \[|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|\leq\varepsilon_f.\] If the original optimizer set is \(X^\star\), each recovered point must also satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(x_i,X^\star)\leq\varepsilon_x\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\). Direct agreement \(\|x_1-x_2\|\leq\varepsilon_x\) is required only when uniqueness or a common selection rule is known; multiple optimal solutions may otherwise yield different but concordant backend outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backend outputs agree when recovered points are valid and near-optimal under common tolerances; distinct points may agree when optima are nonunique.
knowledge_statements.title: Backend Result Concordance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source defines the common-space feasibility, objective, and solution-set tolerances or justifies the stated backend-independent concordance criterion. The distinction between nonunique optimizers and direct pointwise agreement is mathematically appropriate but remains unsupported.

children.title: Status Concordance Across Routes
children.top_down_role: Comparison of translated statuses across canonical representations and solver routes.

assumptions_latex: All routes are exact representations of one original convex problem.
Every route translates statuses by their mathematical semantics rather than backend labels alone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All routes return the same translated exact status whenever that status is mathematically determined by the original problem.

notation.meaning: Route-specific translation to original problem semantics.

review_flags: needs a source connecting exact reformulation equivalence to route-independent status semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concordance of exact mathematical statuses after route-specific translation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Status concordance across routes requires that, for every pair \(r,q\in\mathcal R\) producing certified exact statuses, \[\tau_r(s_r)=\tau_q(s_q).\] In particular, all routes must agree after translation on feasibility, finite optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness. An unknown, iteration-limit, or numerical-failure outcome is not a contradictory mathematical status. A disagreement between certified exact statuses refutes at least one asserted premise: exact representation, status translation, certificate validity, or the route's regularity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact routes must yield the same translated mathematical status; unknown or numerical-failure outputs do not by themselves contradict another route.
knowledge_statements.title: Status Concordance Across Routes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the claim that exact routes must produce identical translated statuses under the stated premises. This requires precise definitions of certified exact status and route-specific regularity, closure, and attainment assumptions.

children.title: Certificate Concordance Across Routes
children.top_down_role: Comparison of recovered certificate meaning across representations and backends.

assumptions_latex: Each route produces a certificate for the same original mathematical claim.
Route-specific recovery maps return certificates in a shared original-space certificate domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recovered certificates from every route validate the same claim under one common original-space predicate.

notation.meaning: Certificate and recovery map for route r.
Common original-space certificate predicate for claim s.

review_flags: needs a source formalizing cross-representation certificate comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic, rather than coordinatewise, agreement of certificates recovered from different routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Certificate concordance across routes holds for claim \(s\) when every route \(r\in\mathcal R\) satisfies \[V_P(P,s,R_r(w_r))=\mathrm{true}.\] The recovered certificates need not be equal: dual multipliers may be nonunique and lifted routes may introduce different auxiliary components. Concordance concerns the certified original-space fact and its residual equations. If certificates are normalized rays, any comparison must quotient out positive scaling; if they are optimal multipliers, comparison may instead use feasibility, objective value, and complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route certificates agree when each recovered object verifies the same original claim, even if multipliers, auxiliary coordinates, or ray scalings differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Concordance Across Routes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source formalizes semantic comparison of recovered certificates across representations, including ray scaling and nonunique multipliers. The record states a concordance condition rather than an actual certificate, so condition is the better content kind once sourced.

children.title: Cross-Route Disagreement Triage
children.top_down_role: Localization of discrepancies to representation, interface, solver, or recovery layers.

assumptions_latex: At least two routes yield outputs that fail a stated concordance check.
Original-space residuals, route metadata, and recovered certificates are available for inspection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a reproducible discrepancy classification or an unresolved case with the failed checks recorded.

notation.meaning: Collection of route outputs and recovery metadata.

review_flags: needs a canonicalization-system reference defining the diagnostic ordering and classifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic triage of result, status, or certificate disagreements between canonicalization routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\mathcal O\), evaluate in order: identical parameter data; domain validity; exact-representation invariants; original-space primal residuals; translated statuses; recovered certificate predicates; and common-tolerance objective residuals. Let \(j=\min\{k:D_k(\mathcal O)=\mathrm{false}\}\). Return the classification attached to \(D_j\): stale data, domain error, reformulation error, recovery error, status error, certificate error, or numerical disagreement. If no predicate fails but outputs still differ, return unresolved nonuniqueness or tolerance mismatch together with all residuals. The output includes \(j\), the implicated routes, parameter hashes, tolerances, and failed equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Triage checks shared data, representation, recovery, status, certificates, and numerical residuals in order, returning the first reproducible failure classification.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Route Disagreement Triage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagnostic ordering, first-failure rule, and classification labels are system-specific algorithmic choices with no supporting source. A canonicalization-system specification is needed before this algorithm can be relied upon.

children.title: Parameter-Update Consistency Checks
children.top_down_role: Validation of cached and incrementally updated canonical data.

assumptions_latex: A fixed canonicalization graph depends on a parameter vector and stores parameter-independent structure separately from numerical data.
Full rebuilding and incremental updating use the same arithmetic and deterministic ordering conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An incremental update is accepted exactly when its canonical data and invariants match a full rebuild for the new parameter value.

notation.meaning: Canonical data produced by a full build at parameter p.
Incremental update of cached canonical data from p to q.

review_flags: needs a source for cached and incremental canonicalization validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential validation of cached canonical data after parameter changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given old parameters \(p\), new parameters \(q\), cached data \(K(p)\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\), compute \(K_{\mathrm{inc}}=U(K(p),p,q)\) and independently compute \(K_{\mathrm{full}}=K(q)\). Compare dimensions, cone blocks, sparsity pattern, variable and constraint maps, and all numerical arrays. Require exact equality for structural data and \[\|K_{\mathrm{inc}}-K_{\mathrm{full}}\|_{\mathrm{scaled}}\leq\varepsilon\] for numerical data. Then run identical domain, recovery, and objective tests on both forms. Accept the cache update only if every comparison passes; otherwise invalidate the affected cache entries and report the first mismatched dependency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate an incremental parameter update by comparing it with a full rebuild, checking structure exactly and numerical data under a declared tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Update Consistency Checks
